title: Food chains and food webs: who eats whom

summary.text: You can see hundreds of ants in a day, but a whole forest may hold only a handful of tigers. The reason is who eats whom. A food chain shows how food passes from a plant to the animal that eats it, and on to the next eater. At each step, the eater uses most of its food just to stay alive, so only about a tenth passes on. Most animals eat several things, so chains join up into food webs, and taking one living thing away changes many others.
summary.art: A bright web drawn on a notebook page: grass and a neem tree at the bottom, grasshoppers, a caterpillar, a frog, a bulbul, a snake and a hawk joined by arrows, with the Sun shining at the top corner.

intro.hook: Look out of a window or at a garden for two minutes. Can you find one living thing that is eating, or hunting? What is it eating? And who might eat it?
intro.text: Right now, somewhere near you, a lizard is waiting by a light for a moth. A caterpillar is chewing a leaf. A crow is pecking at something on the road. Each of them is part of a long line of eating that starts with sunlight on a leaf. Scientists call that line a food chain. In this unit, you will find the chains around your own home. You will see why there are so many ants and so few tigers. And you will find out what happened when a whole country decided that one small bird was its enemy.
intro.art: A window frame with three small scenes outside: a house gecko by a tube light with a moth, a green caterpillar on a leaf, and a crow on a wall.

outcomes: I can say what a food chain is, and draw one of four or five links that starts with a plant, with each arrow pointing to the eater.
I can use the words producer, consumer, herbivore, carnivore, omnivore, predator, prey, scavenger and decomposer, with examples from India.
I can explain what a food web is, and predict what may happen when one living thing is taken away.
I can explain that only about a tenth of the food's energy passes on at each step, and why there are many plants and only a few tigers.
I can run a fair test or a careful count about who eats what, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain how a poison can build up as it passes along a food chain, using the stories of DDT and India's vultures.
I can say what scientists agree on, and what they still argue about: how much one animal changes a whole place, whether nature has a balance, and why food chains are short.

terms.meaning: A line that shows who eats whom. Food passes from one living thing to the next.
terms.example: Grass, then grasshopper, then frog, then snake, then eagle.
terms.art: Five pictures in a row joined by arrows: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, eagle.

terms.meaning: The arrow points from the food to the eater. You can read it as 'is eaten by'. It shows which way the food goes.
terms.example: Grass → goat means the grass is eaten by the goat.
terms.art: A tuft of grass with a big arrow pointing to a goat.

terms.meaning: A living thing that makes its own food. Green plants and algae are producers. They use sunlight, air and water.
terms.example: Grass, a mango tree, rice plants and the green slime in a pond are all producers.
terms.art: A grass tuft, a mango tree and pond algae, each with a small sun above it.

terms.meaning: A living thing that cannot make its own food, so it eats other living things.
terms.example: A cow, a frog, a crow and you are all consumers.
terms.art: A cow eating grass, a frog catching a fly, and a child eating a roti.

terms.meaning: An animal that eats only plants.
terms.example: Cows, goats, chital deer, grasshoppers and caterpillars are herbivores.
terms.art: A chital deer nibbling leaves.

terms.meaning: An animal that eats other animals.
terms.example: Tigers, frogs, spiders, snakes and owls are carnivores.
terms.art: A spider wrapping a fly in its web.

terms.meaning: An animal that eats both plants and animals.
terms.example: Crows, sloth bears, monkeys, hens and most people are omnivores.
terms.art: A crow with a piece of roti in its beak and a worm at its feet.

terms.meaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
terms.example: A kingfisher is a predator of small fish.
terms.art: A kingfisher diving into a pond.

terms.meaning: An animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator.
terms.example: A small fish is the prey of a kingfisher.
terms.art: A small fish darting away under the water.

terms.meaning: An animal that eats animals that are already dead.
terms.example: Vultures, crows, jackals and many ants are scavengers.
terms.art: Vultures standing around a dead buffalo in a dry field.

terms.meaning: A living thing that breaks down dead plants and animals into simple materials, called nutrients. The nutrients go back into the soil, and plants take them in.
terms.example: Mushrooms, mould and bacteria are decomposers. Earthworms help them.
terms.art: A rotting log with mushrooms on it and an earthworm in the soil below.

terms.meaning: Many food chains joined together. It shows that most animals eat, and are eaten by, more than one kind of living thing.
terms.example: A frog eats grasshoppers, flies and spiders. Snakes and herons both eat frogs.
terms.art: A tangle of arrows joining pond animals: algae, mosquito larvae, tadpoles, small fish, frog, heron, snake.

terms.meaning: What it takes to move, grow, keep warm and stay alive. Food carries energy from one living thing to the next.
terms.example: When you run, your body uses energy from the food you ate.
terms.art: A child running, with a little glow passing from a plate of food into the child.

terms.meaning: A drawing that shows how much food energy there is at each step of a food chain. The bottom step, the plants, is the biggest. Each step up is about ten times smaller.
terms.example: A meadow has far more grass than grasshoppers, and far more grasshoppers than frogs.
terms.art: A pyramid of four layers: a wide green layer of grass, then grasshoppers, then frogs, then one snake at the tiny top.

terms.meaning: A predator that no other wild animal usually hunts when it is grown up. It is the last link in its food chain.
terms.example: A tiger in an Indian forest, or a crocodile in a river.
terms.art: A tiger resting under a sal tree.

terms.meaning: A living thing that many others depend on, far more than its numbers suggest. If it disappears, many other living things change. It is named after the keystone at the top of a stone arch, which keeps the other stones in place.
terms.example: A starfish on a rocky shore in America, and vultures in India.
terms.art: A stone arch with its top stone glowing, and a starfish drawn on that stone.

terms.meaning: When a poison builds up more and more as it passes up a food chain. A big eater takes in the poison from every small thing it eats.
terms.example: A poison sprayed on insects ended up thousands of times stronger in fish-eating birds.
terms.art: A row of bottles getting darker: water, tiny plankton, small fish, big fish, an osprey.

terms.meaning: All the living things in one place, together with the water, soil, air and light they use.
terms.example: A pond, with its algae, fish, frogs, mud and water, is an ecosystem.
terms.art: A cut-away pond showing mud, water, plants, fish, a frog and the sky above.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see. When one living thing eats another, its atoms move into the eater.
terms.example: Some of the atoms in a tiger were once in the grass a deer ate.
terms.art: A zoom from a blade of grass to a cluster of tiny coloured balls.

terms.meaning: A kind of atom that every living thing is built from. Plants take it from the air. Animals get it by eating.
terms.example: When you breathe out, some carbon from your breakfast goes back into the air.
terms.art: A small black ball labelled C floating from a child's breath towards a tree.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what made the difference.
terms.example: Put sugar, salt and roti the same distance from the ants, at the same time.
terms.art: Four small paper squares in a row on a floor, each with a different food, an ant trail nearby.

explanations.definition: A food chain shows who eats whom in one place. Each arrow points from the food to the eater.
explanations.description: Start with a plant. Something eats the plant. Something else eats that animal. Write each one down, with an arrow between them. The arrow means 'is eaten by'. It also shows which way the food, and its energy, is going. A common mistake is to point the arrow at the food, like a finger pointing at dinner. Scientists point it the other way, towards the mouth that eats. The British scientist Charles Elton made food chains famous in his book Animal Ecology, in 1927. Long before him, around 1,200 years ago, the Arab writer Al-Jahiz wrote a Book of Animals. In it, he described animals hunting to eat, and being hunted.
examples: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.
Rice plant → rat → rat snake → hawk.
Algae → mosquito larva → small fish → kingfisher.
explanations.art: A notebook page with the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle, and a small speech bubble on the first arrow saying 'is eaten by'.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a food chain is, and which way its arrows point.

explanations.definition: Producers make their own food from sunlight, air and water. Consumers eat other living things. Almost every food chain starts with a producer.
explanations.description: Green plants and algae are producers. Their leaves catch sunlight and use it to build sugar out of air and water. Every animal is a consumer, because no animal can do that. Herbivores eat plants. Carnivores eat animals. Omnivores eat both. So when a tiger eats a deer, it is really eating grass that the deer turned into deer. And the grass was built with sunlight. There are a few strange chains that start in the dark. Deep in the sea, tiny living things make food from chemicals in the rocks instead of from light. So do tiny living things in a sealed cave in Romania, called Movile Cave.
examples: A mango tree is a producer. A parrot eating its fruit is a herbivore, which is a kind of consumer.
You are an omnivore if you eat dal and rice, and also eggs or fish.
Pond algae, the green slime on a pond, are producers. They are the first link in most pond food chains.
explanations.art: The Sun shining on a leaf, an arrow to a deer, an arrow to a tiger, with the words producer and consumer below.
explanations.context: Why does almost every food chain start with a plant? This card explains producers, which make food, and consumers, which eat it.

explanations.concept: Food webs: chains that join up
explanations.definition: A food web is many food chains joined together. It shows everything that eats, and is eaten by, each living thing in one place.
explanations.description: Real animals rarely eat just one thing. A frog eats grasshoppers, flies, spiders and beetles. A frog is eaten by snakes, herons, owls and even big fish. Draw all of these arrows and the chains cross and join, like threads in a fishing net. That net is a food web. Webs are useful because they show something chains hide. If one food runs out, an animal can often switch to another. A web with many threads is harder to break than a single chain. Real webs are huge. Some scientists count every link, even tiny worms that live inside other animals. They find thousands of arrows in one small lake.
examples: A crow eats roti, insects, frogs, eggs and dead animals. It shows up in many chains at once.
If a garden has fewer caterpillars one year, a bulbul can eat more fruit and spiders instead.
explanations.art: Several food chains drawn in different colours, crossing and joining into one web around a garden pond.
explanations.context: Most animals eat more than one thing. This card shows how food chains join up into a food web.

explanations.concept: Scavengers and decomposers: the clean-up crew
explanations.definition: Scavengers eat animals that are already dead. Decomposers break dead things down into nutrients that go back into the soil.
explanations.description: Every living thing dies in the end, even a tiger. What eats it then? First come the scavengers: vultures, jackals, crows and ants. Then the decomposers: fungi, like mould and mushrooms, and bacteria, too small to see. Earthworms and woodlice help by chopping dead leaves into small pieces. The decomposers turn the dead body into simple things that plants can take in through their roots. So the end of every food chain feeds the beginning again. You will learn much more about this in the unit on decomposers.
examples: A dead buffalo in a field: vultures, then flies and beetles, then bacteria and fungi.
Fallen neem leaves in a garden become soil in a few months, because of fungi, bacteria and worms.
explanations.art: A circle: a tiger, a dead tiger with beetles and mushrooms around it, dark soil, then grass growing, then a deer eating the grass.
explanations.context: What happens at the end of a food chain, when the top animal dies? This card is about the living things that eat the dead.

explanations.concept: Only about one tenth passes on
explanations.definition: At each step of a food chain, only about one tenth of the food's energy passes on to the eater. The rest is used up for living, and most of it ends up as heat.
explanations.description: A grasshopper eats a lot of grass. But most of that grass does not become grasshopper. The grasshopper uses most of its food to hop, to breathe, to stay alive and to keep its body working. Some of the grass comes out as poo. And much of the grass is never eaten at all: it dies, and decomposers use it. Only a small part is built into new grasshopper body. So when a frog eats that grasshopper, it gets only that small part. Scientists measured this in the 1930s and 1940s. A young American scientist, Raymond Lindeman, measured the food at each step in a small lake in Minnesota. His paper was first turned down by reviewers. He died in 1942, aged 27, just before it came out. Today it is one of the most famous papers in ecology. The real share is often between one twentieth and one fifth. Scientists round it to one tenth, so it is easy to remember.
examples: If the grass in a field holds 1,000 units of food energy, the grasshoppers get about 100, the frogs about 10, and the snakes about 1.
You get warm when you run. That warmth is food energy leaving your body. It can never be passed on to anything that eats you.
explanations.art: Four bowls in a row, each smaller than the one before: a big heap of grass, a smaller heap of grasshoppers, a few frogs, one thin snake, with wavy heat lines rising from each bowl.
explanations.context: Remember the One Hundred Grains activity, where only one grain in ten passed to the next animal? This card explains why food runs out so fast as it goes up a chain.

chart.note: These are rounded numbers, to show the one-tenth pattern. Real numbers vary.

explanations.concept: Why there are many plants and few tigers
explanations.definition: So little food passes up each step. So there is much more life at the bottom of a food chain than at the top. Scientists draw this as a pyramid.
explanations.description: Picture a forest in Madhya Pradesh. It has millions of grass plants and trees. It has thousands of deer. It has only a few tigers. A tiger eats about one deer-sized animal a week. That is about 50 a year. Tiger scientists in India, such as K. Ullas Karanth, have done the sums. To feed one tiger year after year, a forest needs about 500 deer and other prey animals alive at any time. And those 500 deer need a huge amount of grass and leaves. So a top predator needs a lot of land. That is why tigers need big forests, and why they are often the first to disappear when forests shrink. Charles Elton called this the pyramid of numbers, in 1927.
examples: One tiger, about 500 deer and other prey, and more grass and leaves than you could count.
In a garden: hundreds of leaves, dozens of caterpillars, a few spiders, one bulbul.
explanations.art: A pyramid drawn as a forest: a wide base of grass and trees, a middle band of chital deer, and one tiger at the top.
explanations.context: Have you ever wondered why you see crowds of ants but almost never a tiger? This card explains it with a pyramid.

show.art: A tiger walking through a large forest seen from above, with small dots for deer spread across it.
show.caption: One tiger needs a big forest full of deer.

show.art: A wide meadow of grass with a few deer grazing.
show.caption: And the deer need wide meadows of grass.

explanations.description: Most food chains have only three, four or five links. Hardly any have more than six. Why not ten? Scientists have asked this since at least 1959, when the ecologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson wrote about it. They still argue about the answer.
examples: Grass → deer → tiger has only three links.
In the open sea, chains are often longer: tiny algae → tiny shrimps → small fish → bigger fish → tuna → shark.

perspectives.who: The energy idea, from the one-tenth rule
perspectives.explanation: Each step passes on only about a tenth of the food energy. After five or six steps, there is too little food left to feed a big animal that hunts further up.

perspectives.who: Stuart Pimm and John Lawton, in 1977, and others
perspectives.explanation: Long chains are wobbly. If something goes wrong near the bottom, the shock grows as it travels up. So animals far up long chains die out more easily.
The size of the place matters most. They studied lakes and found that bigger lakes had longer food chains. A small pond cannot hold enough food for a big top predator.

explanations.art: A long ladder of animals that wobbles and fades out at the top, next to a short, steady chain of three links.
explanations.context: Food chains almost never have more than five or six links. This card is about why, which scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: Predators and prey keep changing each other
explanations.definition: The number of predators depends on how much prey there is. The number of prey depends on how many predators hunt them. So the two often rise and fall in turns.
explanations.description: Imagine a forest with lots of deer. The tigers eat well and raise many cubs. More tigers eat more deer, so the deer become fewer. Now the tigers go hungry, and fewer cubs survive. With fewer tigers, the deer increase again. Scientists saw this pattern in old fur-trading records from Canada, which go back more than 100 years. They counted the furs of lynx, a wild cat, and of snowshoe hares, its prey. Roughly every ten years, the hares became many, then the lynx became many, then both crashed. Charles Elton studied these records. Today scientists know that the hares' food, and their sicknesses, also play a part.
examples: Lynx and snowshoe hares in Canada rise and fall about every ten years.
In the Deer and Tiger Toss game, the deer rise first, then the tigers, then the deer fall.
explanations.art: A wavy line chart with two lines, a tall one for hares and a lower one for lynx, rising and falling one after the other, with a lynx and a hare drawn beside it.
explanations.context: Do predators and prey affect each other's numbers? This card explains how they rise and fall in turns.

chart.title: Deer and tigers in the Deer and Tiger Toss game (made-up example)
chart.note: Made-up results from the game, to show the pattern. The deer rise first. Then the tigers rise. Then the deer fall, and the tigers fall after them.

explanations.concept: Keystone species: one animal that many others depend on
explanations.definition: A keystone species is a living thing that many others depend on, far more than its numbers suggest. Take it away and the whole place changes.
explanations.description: From 1963, the American ecologist Robert Paine did a simple test on a rocky shore in Washington State. On one stretch of rock, he kept pulling off the purple starfish and throwing them into the sea. He left a nearby stretch alone. The starfish eat mussels. Without them, the mussels spread and covered the rock. They crowded out barnacles, limpets and seaweed. Within a few years, the number of kinds of living things on his stretch fell from 15 to 8. In 1969 he named such animals keystone species. Sea otters are another example. They eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat giant seaweed called kelp. Where otters were hunted away, the urchins ate the kelp forests down to bare rock. India has its own keystone story, about vultures. You will find it on another card.
examples: Remove the starfish, and the mussels take over the shore.
Remove the sea otters, and the kelp forests disappear.
explanations.art: Two rocky shores side by side: one with starfish and many kinds of shells and seaweed, one covered only in mussels.
explanations.context: What happens if you take just one kind of animal out of a food web? This card tells the story of a scientist who tried it on purpose.

explanations.description: Wolves were killed off in Yellowstone National Park in America by the 1920s. Elk, a kind of large deer, then grew many and ate the young willow and aspen trees along the rivers. In 1995 and 1996, scientists brought wolves back. Elk numbers fell, and some trees began to grow again. Scientists call a chain of changes like this, passing down a food chain, a trophic cascade. A popular video says the wolves even changed the shape of the rivers. Scientists argue about how much of this is true.
examples: Wolves eat elk. Elk eat young willow trees. Willow trees hold river banks in place.

perspectives.who: William Ripple, Robert Beschta and others
perspectives.explanation: The wolves set off a cascade. Elk ate fewer young trees, so willows and aspens grew back along some rivers.

perspectives.who: Matthew Kauffman, Tom Hobbs and others
perspectives.explanation: The effect is much smaller and patchier than the popular story says. In many places, the trees did not come back. Other causes matter too, such as bears, cougars, people hunting elk, dry years, and beavers that went missing from the rivers.
The wolves made some difference. How big it was, and whether it reached the rivers, is still argued.

explanations.art: A wolf on a snowy hill above a river with willow trees, with a big question mark over the river.
explanations.context: Can one predator change a whole national park? This card is about a famous story that scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: Poisons can build up as they go up a chain
explanations.definition: Some poisons do not wash out of an animal's body. So a predator collects the poison from every animal it eats. The poison builds up more and more at each step. This is called biomagnification.
explanations.description: In the 1940s and 1950s, farmers and towns sprayed a chemical called DDT to kill insects. A little of it washed into rivers and lakes. Tiny water plants and animals took in a little. Small fish ate thousands of them. Big fish ate hundreds of small fish. Fish-eating birds, like ospreys and eagles, ate many big fish. In the birds' bodies, the DDT was many thousands of times stronger than in the water. It made their eggshells so thin that the eggs broke when the parents sat on them. The American scientist and writer Rachel Carson told the world in her book Silent Spring, in 1962. Chemical companies attacked her and called her hysterical. She was very ill with cancer while she defended her work. Her evidence held up. DDT was banned for farming in the United States in 1972, and later in many other countries.
examples: DDT: water, then plankton, then small fish, then big fish, then eggs that broke under ospreys.
Today, people are told to eat big sea fish like shark and swordfish only sometimes. Mercury, a metal, builds up in them in the same way.
explanations.art: A food chain from water to plankton to small fish to big fish to an osprey, with the DDT drawn as red dots, a few at the start and crowds of them in the osprey's cracked egg.
explanations.context: Remember the Poison Climbs the Chain activity, with beads passed up from plankton to fish to heron? This card tells the real story behind it.

explanations.concept: India's vultures: a medicine that passed one step up
explanations.definition: In the 1990s and early 2000s, India lost more than 95 out of every 100 of its vultures. A medicine given to sick cattle was poisoning the vultures that ate the cattle after they died.
explanations.description: Vultures used to gather in hundreds wherever a cow or buffalo died. They could clean a body to the bones in less than an hour. Then they began to die. An Indian bird scientist, Vibhu Prakash of the Bombay Natural History Society, was one of the first to notice. He had counted 353 pairs of nesting vultures in Keoladeo National Park, in Bharatpur, in the late 1980s. Within a few years the colony had crashed, and by the early 2000s it was gone. In 2004, scientists led by Lindsay Oaks showed the cause. It was diclofenac, a painkiller given to cattle. It stayed in the dead animals, and it destroyed the vultures' kidneys. This is not quite the slow build-up of DDT. One meal was enough. But it shows how what an animal eats passes up the web. India banned diclofenac for animals in 2006. Vets now use a medicine called meloxicam, which is safe for vultures. Without vultures, dead cattle lay rotting, and the number of street dogs grew. More people were bitten, and more caught rabies. In 2024, two economists, Eyal Frank and Anant Sudarshan, made an estimate. They think the loss of vultures led to about half a million extra human deaths between 2000 and 2005. That number is an estimate, and other scientists are still checking it.
examples: Sick cow → painkiller → dead cow → vulture: the medicine passed one step up the chain.
Fewer vultures → more rotting carcasses → more dogs → more dog bites and rabies.
explanations.art: Two scenes: many vultures on a dead buffalo in a dry field in the 1980s, and the same field years later with a pack of dogs and no vultures.
explanations.context: Vultures were once common all over India. This card explains how a medicine for cattle nearly wiped them out, and what changed after they went.

explanations.concept: Atoms go round, energy flows through
explanations.definition: When one living thing eats another, its atoms move into the eater. Atoms are used again and again for ever. But the energy is used only once. It leaves as heat and does not come back.
explanations.description: Follow one carbon atom. Today it floats in the air. Tomorrow a blade of grass takes it in through a leaf and builds it into sugar. A goat eats the grass. The atom becomes part of the goat. One day the goat dies, and decomposers break it down. The atom goes back into the air, ready for another leaf. Atoms go round and round like this for millions of years. Energy is different. It arrives from the Sun as light. Plants store some of it in food. At each step of the chain, most of it turns into heat. That heat spreads out and slowly leaves the Earth as invisible light, into space. So life needs a fresh supply of sunlight every day. And the Sun's light itself comes from deep inside the Sun, where tiny hydrogen atoms are squeezed together to make helium.
examples: Some of the carbon atoms in your body were in plants a few months ago. Some were in the air last year.
Without sunlight, plants would stop making new food. Animals would eat what was left, and then the whole chain would starve.
explanations.art: A circle of arrows carrying a small black carbon atom from air to grass to goat to soil and back to air, with a straight golden arrow of sunlight coming in at the top and red heat lines leaving towards space.
explanations.context: Food carries two things from one living thing to the next: atoms and energy. This card shows how they travel in different ways.

explanations.concept: Where are humans in the food web?
explanations.definition: People often say humans are at the top of the food chain. Scientists who measured what people actually eat found that, on average, we are much lower down.
explanations.description: Scientists give each living thing a number for how far up the food chain it is. Plants are 1. Animals that eat only plants are 2. Animals that eat those animals are 3, and so on. A tiger or a killer whale is about 4 or 5. In 2013, scientists led by Sylvain Bonhommeau worked out the number for humans. They used what people around the world eat. It was about 2.2. That is close to a pig or an anchovy, a small fish. This is because most of what people eat is rice, wheat, dal, vegetables and other plants. So what puts humans 'on top' is not what we eat. It is how strongly we change every food web on Earth, by farming, fishing, cutting forests and building cities.
examples: A family that eats mostly rice, dal and vegetables is eating close to the bottom of the food chain.
Fishing boats catch so many big fish that some sea food webs now have fewer top predators than before.
explanations.art: A ladder numbered 1 to 5 with a plant on 1, a goat on 2, a frog on 3, a tiger on 4 and 5, and a child standing near step 2, holding a plate of rice and dal.
explanations.context: People often say humans are at the top of the food chain. This card checks whether that is true.

explanations.concept: Is there a balance of nature?
explanations.description: People have long said that nature has a balance: if nothing disturbs it, every animal stays in the right number. Scientists today are less sure. They argue about what 'balance' means, and whether it exists.
examples: Fire, floods and storms change forests all the time, even without people.
Some grasslands with many kinds of plants recovered better after a drought than grasslands with only a few kinds.

perspectives.who: The old idea, still common in books
perspectives.explanation: Nature is like a set of scales. Predators, prey and plants keep each other at the right numbers. The web stays the same for ever, unless people spoil it.

perspectives.who: Daniel Botkin, an American ecologist, in his book Discordant Harmonies (1990), and many ecologists since
perspectives.explanation: There is no fixed balance. Nature changes all the time, through fire, storms, disease and chance. Webs wobble and shift. What matters is whether they can keep going through the changes.

perspectives.who: Robert May, an Australian scientist, in 1972, and David Tilman, an American ecologist, in the 1990s
perspectives.explanation: They disagree with each other in an interesting way. May's maths suggested that a web with very many links can be less steady, not more. Tilman's grassland experiments found that fields with more kinds of plants stayed steadier through a drought. Both may be right in different situations.

explanations.art: A set of old weighing scales with a tiger on one side and deer on the other, beside a wobbling spinning top made of animals.
explanations.context: Does nature keep itself in balance? This card is about a big idea that scientists still argue about.

agreed.text: Almost every food chain starts with a producer: a green plant or algae that makes food from sunlight.
agreed.evidence: Animals have never been seen making their own food from light. Cut off the light to a pond, and its algae die first, then everything that eats them.

agreed.text: Only a small part of the food's energy, often about a tenth, passes on at each step. The rest is used for living and ends as heat.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured it in lakes, fields, forests and the sea since Raymond Lindeman's lake study, published in 1942.

agreed.text: Most animals eat more than one thing, so food chains join up into food webs.
agreed.evidence: When scientists look inside the stomachs of wild animals, or film what they eat, they nearly always find several kinds of food.

agreed.text: Removing one living thing from a web can change many others, sometimes a lot.
agreed.evidence: Robert Paine's starfish test on a rocky shore, the sea otters and kelp of the Pacific, and the loss of India's vultures.

agreed.text: Some poisons build up as they pass up a food chain.
agreed.evidence: DDT was measured in water, plankton, fish and birds. It was weakest in the water and strongest in the birds at the top. Ospreys' and eagles' eggshells got thinner, then thicker again after DDT was banned.

challenging.claim: The tiger is the king of the forest. The top of the food chain is the strongest, most important place to be.
challenging.who: A common way of thinking, in stories and films
challenging.for: Nothing hunts a grown tiger. It can kill animals much bigger than itself.
challenging.against: The tiger is the most dependent animal in the forest. It needs about 500 prey animals, and they need huge meadows. If the grass fails, the tiger starves. If the tiger disappears, the grass still grows. When a tiger dies, beetles, fungi and bacteria eat it.
challenging.context: This card questions a common idea: that the animal at the top of a food chain is the most powerful.

challenging.claim: Predators are bad. Killing them helps the deer and the forest.
challenging.who: Many governments and hunters, in the early 1900s
challenging.for: Predators kill deer and farm animals. Without them, more deer survive.
challenging.against: On the Kaibab Plateau in Arizona, in America, hunters killed thousands of predators between 1906 and the 1930s. They killed cougars, coyotes and the last wolves. The famous story says the deer then grew so many that they ate the forest bare and starved. Later scientists, such as Graeme Caughley in 1970, showed the deer counts were guesses, and sheep and cattle grazing also changed things. So the story is less clear than it seemed. But many other studies show that removing predators often lets plant-eaters strip their food.
challenging.context: Should we get rid of predators to help the animals they hunt? This card is about a famous story, and how it was later questioned.

challenging.claim: Wolves brought back to Yellowstone changed the shape of its rivers.
challenging.who: A popular online video, 'How Wolves Change Rivers', made in 2014 and watched millions of times
challenging.for: After wolves returned in 1995, elk numbers fell and some willows along rivers grew back. Willow roots hold river banks.
challenging.against: Many ecologists say the video goes too far. In many places, the trees did not come back, and other changes, like fewer beavers and drier years, matter a lot. Nobody has shown that the rivers' shape changed because of the wolves.
challenging.context: Can one predator change a river? This card is about a much-loved video that scientists say goes too far.

challenging.claim: Chief Seattle said: 'Man did not weave the web of life. He is merely a strand in it.'
challenging.who: Posters, books and websites all over the world
challenging.for: Chief Seattle was a real leader of the Suquamish and Duwamish peoples, in what is now Washington State. He gave a real speech in 1854.
challenging.against: Nobody wrote down his speech at the time in his own language. The words about the web of life were written by an American screenwriter, Ted Perry, for a film in 1971. The idea is beautiful. But the quote is not Chief Seattle's.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous quote about the web of life, and who really wrote it. It is a lesson in checking where words come from.

challenging.claim: Nature is a war of everyone against everyone. Eating and being eaten is all there is.
challenging.who: The poet Alfred Tennyson wrote of nature 'red in tooth and claw', in 1850. Many people read early books about evolution in this way.
challenging.for: Every animal must eat, and most are eaten in the end. Predators do hunt and kill.
challenging.against: Webs are full of helping too. Bees feed on flowers and carry their pollen. Fungi in the soil pass food to tree roots. In 1902, Peter Kropotkin, a Russian thinker, wrote a book called Mutual Aid. He argued that animals helping each other matters as much as competing. Scientists today agree that both happen everywhere.
challenging.context: Is nature only about hunting and being hunted? This card looks at an old view, and at the evidence for helping.

challenging.claim: Eating more plant food, and less meat, means the same land can feed more people.
challenging.for: Only about a tenth of the energy passes up each step. So plants eaten by people feed about ten times more people than the same plants fed to animals first.
challenging.against: Some land, like steep hills and dry grassland, cannot grow crops, but goats, sheep and cattle can graze it. Animal foods also give some nutrients that are harder to get from plants alone. So the exact numbers depend on the place.
challenging.context: This card uses the one-tenth rule to ask a real question about feeding the world.

big_questions.q: If a tiger eats a deer, and the deer ate grass, is the tiger partly made of grass?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the tiger's atoms came from. Did any of them come from the tiger itself?

big_questions.q: Where does the energy go when a frog hops? Can it ever come back?
big_questions.hint: Run on the spot for one minute. Where does your warmth go afterwards?

big_questions.q: Why do you think almost no food chain has more than six links?
big_questions.hint: Remember the One Hundred Grains. How much was left after five steps?

big_questions.q: Is the top of the food chain the best place to be?
big_questions.hint: Who needs whom more: the tiger or the grass?

big_questions.q: Every animal eats, and most are eaten. Is that cruel? Or is it part of how life keeps going?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to a forest where nothing ever died, and nothing was ever eaten?

big_questions.q: A whole country once decided that sparrows were its enemy. How can we tell if a living thing is really a 'pest'?
big_questions.hint: What does it eat? And who would eat that, if it were gone?

big_questions.q: Rachel Carson was attacked for saying a useful chemical was harming birds. Why is it hard to listen to news we do not want to hear?
big_questions.hint: Who was making money from the chemical? Who could not speak for themselves?

big_questions.q: Where are you in the food web? What eats you?
big_questions.hint: Think about mosquitoes, the tiny living things in your gut, and what happens to every body in the end.

big_questions.q: Vultures and decomposers do the work nobody wants to do. Who does that work among people? Do we thank them?
big_questions.hint: Who cleans the streets, collects the rubbish and cleans the drains near you?

big_questions.q: Is there a balance of nature, or does nature just keep changing?
big_questions.hint: Is your own family exactly the same as five years ago? Is it still a family?

big_questions.q: The same atoms go round and round through living things. Could an atom in your finger once have been in a dinosaur?
big_questions.hint: Atoms last for billions of years. Dinosaurs lived about 66 million years ago and more.

story.title: The Year We Chased the Sparrows
story.note: The Four Pests campaign of 1958 in China is real. So is the way sparrows were hunted, by people banging pots on roofs until the birds fell from tiredness. The bird scientist Zheng Zuoxin (also spelled Tso-hsin Cheng) is real. His team studied what sparrows ate, found many insects, especially in spring, and spoke against killing them. He was later punished. In 1960 sparrows were taken off the list and bedbugs added. Insect pests did increase. But historians agree that the great famine of 1959 to 1961 had many causes, mainly the government's farming policies, and the sparrows were only a small part. Lan, her family, old Wu, the nest and the village are made up.
text: In the spring of 1958, in a rice village in the south of China, Lan learned that the little brown sparrows were her enemies.

There were posters on every wall. They showed four pests: the rat, the fly, the mosquito and the sparrow. The sparrow, the posters said, stole the people's grain. If every family killed its sparrows, there would be more rice for everyone. Lan was nine. She had never thought about sparrows at all. They were just there, like the wind, hopping in the dust and arguing on the roof.

Under the eaves of her own house, two sparrows had built a nest of straw and feathers. That spring, Lan sometimes sat on the step and watched them. The parents flew in and out all morning. She noticed something, without thinking much about it. They did not carry rice. They carried small green caterpillars, and once a fat grasshopper with its legs still kicking. The chicks opened their mouths so wide that their heads seemed to be all mouth. Lan counted forty trips before her mother called her in to eat.

Then came the chosen day. At dawn, the whole village climbed onto the roofs. Old people, children, the teacher, the doctor, everyone. Lan was given her mother's iron wok and a ladle. The village headman blew a whistle, and the noise began.

They banged pots and gongs and drums. They waved red flags on long bamboo poles. They shouted until their throats were raw. A sparrow can fly only so long before it must rest. So the sparrows flew up from one roof, and found people banging on the next roof, and the next, and the next. In every village for miles, people were doing the same. There was nowhere to land.

By the afternoon, Lan's arm ached and her ears rang. Small brown birds began to drop out of the sky. They fell onto the threshing floor, into the paddy, at her feet. Some were already dead. She picked one up. It was warm and as light as a dry leaf. Its eyes were closed. The headman's son walked through the lanes with a basket, collecting the bodies to be counted. Lan put her sparrow in the basket. Everyone was cheering. She cheered too, because everyone was.
That evening the nest under the eaves was silent. No parents came. In a day or two, the chicks were quiet too.

The rice grew tall and green that summer. Then, one morning, old Wu next door called out from his field. The leaves of his rice plants were rolled up into tubes and turning brown. Inside each tube was a small green caterpillar. In the next field, tiny insects called planthoppers crowded on the stems, sucking the juice. The farmers went out at night with oil lamps and picked insects off by hand. They filled buckets. In the morning there were just as many.
'Where are they all coming from?' Lan's father said. 'We have never had so many.'

Lan did not answer. She went and stood under the eaves and looked up at the empty nest. She remembered the green caterpillars in the parents' beaks. Forty trips in one morning. And that was only one nest. There had been sparrows on every roof in the village, in every village in the valley.

Something turned over in her mind, like a stone in the river. The sparrows had eaten some rice, yes. But all spring they had also been eating the things that eat rice. Every caterpillar carried to that nest was a caterpillar that would never roll up a rice leaf. The sparrows had been thieves, a little. They had also been guards. Nobody had counted that.
At supper she tried to say it. 'The sparrows ate the caterpillars,' she said. 'Now nobody eats them.'
Her mother put down her bowl and looked at the door. 'Lan,' she said quietly. 'The posters say the sparrow is a pest. Do not say that outside this house.'

So Lan did not say it outside. But in her school notebook, she drew the rice plant. She drew an arrow from the rice to the sparrow. Then she drew an arrow from the rice to the caterpillar, and another arrow from the caterpillar to the sparrow. She looked at it for a long time. The sparrow had two arrows going into it, not one. The posters had only drawn one.

Far away in Beijing, a bird scientist named Zheng Zuoxin had been doing the same thing, with more care. His team cut open hundreds of sparrows and looked at what was in their stomachs. In winter, it was mostly seeds. But in spring and summer, when they fed their chicks, it was full of insects. He told the government that sparrows should not be on the list. For saying so, he was later punished.

The harvest that year was poor, and the next years were worse. Lan's family was hungry for a long time. There were many reasons for the hunger, much bigger than birds. But the insects in old Wu's field were one of them.
In 1960, a new list went up on the walls. The sparrow had been taken off. In its place was the bedbug. When old Wu read it, he laughed, but it was not a happy laugh.

The next spring, Lan was eleven. One morning, sitting on the step, she heard a small dry chirp. A brown bird landed on the edge of the eaves with a piece of straw in its beak. It looked at her sideways. Then it hopped into the old nest.
Lan did not tell anyone. She filled a cracked saucer with water and set it on the windowsill. Then she picked up her basket and went out to help her father in the field.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn is Lan's drawing. The posters drew a food chain with one arrow: rice → sparrow. Lan draws the food web: rice → sparrow, and also rice → caterpillar → sparrow. In a web, an animal can be a thief and a guard at the same time. Take it away, and the things it ate are suddenly free to multiply. The story also asks, gently, what it takes to say something true when everyone around you is cheering for the opposite.
ask: The posters said sparrows eat rice. What else did Lan see the sparrows eating?
Why did the caterpillars and planthoppers increase after the sparrows were gone?
Lan drew two arrows going into the sparrow. What did the second arrow show that the posters missed?
Lan cheered when everyone else cheered. Have you ever done something because everyone else was doing it?
Why do you think Lan put out a saucer of water at the end, without telling anyone?

games.title: Hungry Web

printables.title: 28 living-thing cards to cut out (each card says what it eats)
items: SUN: the start of everything. Goes in the middle.
Grass: a producer. Needs the SUN.
Neem tree: a producer. Needs the SUN.
Rice plant: a producer. Needs the SUN.
Mango tree: a producer. Needs the SUN.
Pond algae: a producer. Needs the SUN.
Flowers: a producer. Needs the SUN.
Caterpillar: eats mango tree leaves, rice plant, flowers.
Chital deer: eats grass, neem tree leaves, mango tree leaves.
Rat: eats rice plant, grass seeds, mango.
Parrot: eats mango, rice plant, neem tree fruit.
Frog: eats grasshopper, caterpillar, honeybee, mosquito larva.
Small fish: eats mosquito larva, pond algae.
Crested serpent eagle: eats rat snake, frog.
Crow: eats rice plant, mango, caterpillar, frog, rat.
Mongoose: eats rat, rat snake, frog, grasshopper.
Human: eats rice plant, mango, small fish, honeybee's honey.
CLEAN-UP Vulture: eats any dead animal. Join to up to 3 animals.
CLEAN-UP Mushroom: eats any dead plant or animal. Join to up to 3 cards.
CLEAN-UP Earthworm: eats dead leaves. Join to up to 3 plants.

printables.title: 40 arrow strips (thin strips of paper, about as long as a finger, with an arrowhead drawn at one end)

rules: Put the SUN card in the middle of the floor. Shuffle the other 27 cards and deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down in a pile.
On your turn, play one card from your hand. Put it near the cards it eats. A producer goes near the SUN.
Lay one arrow strip from each food already on the floor to your card. The arrow always points to the eater. Score 1 point for each arrow.
A CLEAN-UP card can join to up to 3 cards already on the floor, because everything dies in the end. It scores 1 point for each arrow.
If you cannot play, take a card from the pile and miss your turn. If someone lays a wrong arrow, any player can say 'Wrong way!' and take that point.
When nobody can play, the player with the most points wins. Then play the last round: Pull One Card.
Playing alone: play every card yourself, one at a time, as cleverly as you can. Count all your arrows. Write your score and try to beat it next time. The best scores are over 40.

flow.do: 1. Put the SUN card in the middle of the floor. 2. Shuffle the other cards and deal 5 to each player. 3. Put the arrow strips in a bowl.
flow.say: In this game, we build a food web on the floor. Every arrow goes from the food to the eater. The more arrows you can make, the more points you win.
flow.kid: Put the SUN in the middle. Deal 5 cards each. Every arrow goes from the food to the eater. More arrows, more points!
flow.context: This is the first step of Hungry Web. It is a card game where you build a food web on the floor, with paper arrows from each food to its eater.

flow.do: Play the first two cards together as practice. Put Grass next to the SUN with one arrow. Then put Grasshopper next to Grass with one arrow.
flow.say: Let's practise. Grass needs the Sun, so the arrow goes from the Sun to the grass. Now the grasshopper eats the grass. Which way does that arrow point?
flow.kid: Practice! Put Grass by the SUN. Lay an arrow. Now put Grasshopper by the Grass. Which way does the arrow point?

check.q: The grasshopper eats the grass. Which arrow is right?
check.why: In a food chain, the arrow points from the food to the eater. It shows which way the food goes: out of the grass and into the grasshopper. Picking 'Grasshopper → Grass' is very common. It is like a finger pointing at dinner. Scientists draw it the other way, so you can follow the food.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player plays one card and lays arrows from its foods. 2. Count the arrows and write the score. 3. Ask each player to read their new arrows out loud.
flow.say: Read your arrows out loud. For example: the frog eats the grasshopper, and the frog eats the caterpillar. That's two points.
flow.kid: Play a card near its food. Lay an arrow from each food. Read them out loud. One point for each arrow.
flow.parent: Smart players hold back animals that eat many things, like the crow, the frog or the mongoose. They wait until those foods are on the floor. Clean-up cards are best played late, when many animals are out. If a child joins the tiger to the grass, ask: 'Does a tiger eat grass? What does it eat?'

ask.q: Which card made the most arrows? Why?
good: The crow, because it eats lots of different things.
The frog, because many things eat it and it eats many things.

flow.do: Last round, Pull One Card. 1. Choose one card in the web, for example the Frog. 2. Take it out, with all its arrows. 3. Count how many arrows broke. 4. Ask who has lost food, and who has one hunter fewer.
flow.say: Imagine all the frogs disappeared. Let's take the frog out. Which animals have lost some of their food? Which animals now have nobody eating them?
flow.kid: Take the Frog out of the web. How many arrows broke? Who lost some food? Who has one hunter fewer?

check.q: If all the frogs disappeared from a rice field, what would most likely happen to the grasshoppers?
options: They would increase, because fewer animals eat them
check.why: Frogs eat grasshoppers. With no frogs, fewer grasshoppers are eaten, so their numbers usually go up. Then they may eat more of the rice. Picking 'they would all die' usually means thinking that if one animal goes, everything in its chain goes. But the grasshopper did not need the frog. The frog needed the grasshopper.

flow.think: Which card, if you pulled it out, would break the most arrows? Is that the most important living thing in the web?

games.context: This is a card game about food webs. You build a web on the floor, card by card, with a paper arrow from each food to its eater. Then you pull one card out and see what breaks.

setup.caption: 2. Play a card near its food. Arrows point to the eater.

games.title: Deer and Tiger Toss

printables.title: 40 deer squares (cut from paper, each about 2 cm across, the size of a fingernail)
8 tiger squares (cut from thick card, each about 10 cm across, the size of a hand)
The forest: one sheet of A4 paper, or a page of a school notebook opened flat

rules: Put one A4 sheet on the floor. This is the forest.
Round 1: scatter 6 deer squares on the forest. Put 1 tiger on the side.
Hunting: kneel beside the forest. Drop each tiger square from about the height of your head, so it lands on the forest. Every deer it touches is eaten. Take those deer away.
A tiger that ate 0 or 1 deer starves. Take it away. A tiger that ate 2 or 3 survives. A tiger that ate 4 or more survives and also has a cub: add one tiger for the next round.
Then the deer have babies. Count the deer left, and add the same number again. The forest only has grass for 40 deer, so never go over 40.
If all the tigers starve, one new tiger wanders in from the next forest at the start of the next round. If all the deer are eaten, 2 deer wander in.
Write the numbers on the record sheet. Play 12 rounds. Then look at your numbers: what happened to the deer, and to the tigers?

flow.do: 1. Cut 40 small paper squares for deer and 8 hand-sized card squares for tigers. 2. Put one A4 sheet on the floor as the forest. 3. Put 6 deer on the forest and 1 tiger beside it.
flow.say: This paper is a forest. These little squares are deer. This big square is a tiger. Let's see what happens to them over many years.
flow.kid: Cut 40 small deer squares and 8 big tiger squares. One sheet of paper is the forest. Put 6 deer on it. One tiger waits beside it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Deer and Tiger Toss. It is a game about how the numbers of predators and prey change each other, one year at a time.

flow.do: 1. Each round, drop each tiger once from head height onto the forest. 2. Remove the deer it touches. 3. Decide which tigers starve or have a cub. 4. Double the deer that are left, up to 40. 5. Write the numbers on the record sheet. 6. Play 12 rounds.
flow.say: Drop the tiger. How many deer did it catch? Is that enough to survive? Now the deer have babies. Let's write down the numbers.
flow.kid: Drop each tiger from head height. Take away every deer it touches. Did it eat 2? It lives. 4? It has a cub! Then double the deer. Write it down.
flow.parent: The numbers depend on luck, so every game is different. Usually the deer increase for a few rounds while the single tiger struggles. Then, with lots of deer, the tigers catch more and have cubs. With many tigers, the deer fall. Then the tigers starve, and the deer rise again. Each round takes about a minute. If your game does not show this in 12 rounds, play 5 more. If the deer reach 40 and stay there, the tigers will catch up soon. Drop the tigers, don't aim them, or the game stops being fair.

ask.q: Why do the tigers do badly when there are only a few deer?
good: There isn't enough food for them.
The tiger misses because the deer are spread out.

flow.do: Look at the record sheet together. Find the round with the most deer, and the round with the most tigers.
flow.say: Which came first: the most deer, or the most tigers? Why do you think it happened in that order?
flow.kid: Find the round with the most deer. Find the round with the most tigers. Which came first? Why?

check.q: In the game, what usually happens a few rounds after the deer become very many?
options: The tigers increase, then the deer fall
The deer keep growing for ever
check.why: With lots of deer, each dropped tiger lands on more of them. So the tigers eat well, survive and have cubs. More tigers then eat more deer, and the deer fall. Picking 'the tigers all starve' mixes up the order: tigers starve when deer are few, not when they are many. The deer cannot grow for ever, because the forest only has grass for 40.

flow.think: Real scientists found this same pattern in 100 years of fur-trade records of lynx and hares in Canada. How do you think they counted wild animals so long ago?

games.context: This is a game about predators and prey. Paper deer live in a paper forest. Card tigers are dropped onto them to hunt. Over twelve rounds, you watch how the numbers of each change the other.
