items.p: In a food chain, which way does the arrow point?
opts: From the eater to its food
From the food to the eater
From the biggest animal to the smallest
items.why: The arrow points from the food to the eater. It shows which way the food goes. Picking 'from the eater to its food' is the most common mistake: it draws the arrow like a finger pointing at dinner.
items.art: Grass with an arrow pointing to a goat.

items.p: Which of these is a producer?
items.why: A mango tree makes its own food from sunlight, air and water, so it is a producer. Picking the mushroom is a common mix-up, because mushrooms grow from the ground like plants. But a mushroom cannot make food from light. It eats dead things, so it is a decomposer.

items.p: Almost every food chain starts with a green ____.
items.why: Green plants, and algae, make food from sunlight. Animals cannot, so every animal's food comes from a plant in the end.

items.p: Sort these animals. Do they eat plants, animals, or both?
items.why: Deer and grasshoppers eat only plants. Tigers and frogs eat only animals. Crows and sloth bears eat fruit, insects and much more, so they are omnivores.

items.p: Put this food chain in the right order: snake, grass, frog, grasshopper.
items.why: The chain starts with the producer, grass. The grasshopper eats grass, the frog eats the grasshopper, and the snake eats the frog.

items.p: Which of these is a correct food chain?
items.why: Grass is eaten by the deer, and the deer is eaten by the tiger. Picking 'Tiger → deer → grass' means the arrows point at the food instead of at the eater. The chain is right, but backwards.

items.p: Most animals eat only one kind of food.
items.why: False. Most animals eat several kinds of food. That is why food chains join up into food webs.

items.p: Many food chains joined together make a food ____.
items.why: A food web shows all the 'who eats whom' links in one place, crossing like the threads of a net.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: an animal that hunts other animals
an animal that eats animals already dead
a living thing that breaks dead things into soil
items.why: A kingfisher is a predator and a small fish its prey. A vulture is a scavenger. A mushroom is a decomposer.

items.p: A vulture eats a dead buffalo. What is the vulture?
items.why: A scavenger eats animals that are already dead. Picking 'herbivore' usually comes from thinking the buffalo ate grass, which it did. But the vulture eats the buffalo's meat, not grass.

items.p: Look at the chart. Ants came most to the sugar and the roti, and not to the salt. Why?
opts: Sugar and roti came from plants and carry food energy. Salt has none.
Salt is too heavy for ants
items.why: Sugar comes from sugarcane and roti from wheat. Both carry energy a plant made from sunlight. Salt comes from the sea or rocks and gives no energy. Picking 'only like white things' cannot be right: salt is white too, and the ants ignored it.
items.context: In the ant test, you put four paper squares near some ants: one with sugar, one with salt, one with a piece of roti, and one with nothing. Then you count the ants on each.

chart.title: Ants on each square after 30 minutes (made-up results)

items.p: In the ant test, why did we put one square with nothing on it?
opts: To see how many ants walk onto a square just by chance
To give the ants a rest
Because we ran out of food
items.why: The empty square shows how many ants arrive by accident. If the sugar square has many more than the empty one, we know the sugar attracted them. Picking 'to give the ants a rest' is a kind idea, but it would not help us learn anything.
items.context: In the ant test, you put four paper squares near some ants: one with sugar, one with salt, one with a piece of roti, and one with nothing. Then you count the ants on each.

items.p: Which living thing is a decomposer?
items.why: Mould is a fungus. It breaks down the dead bread. Picking 'neem tree' usually means anything that grows is thought of as the same as a fungus. But a neem tree makes its own food from light.

items.p: Write a food chain of four links from near your home. Use arrows that point to the eater.
items.a: Any correct chain that starts with a plant. For example: mango leaf → caterpillar → bulbul → cat.
items.why: A good chain starts with a producer and each arrow points from the food to its eater.

items.p: Draw a food web with at least five living things from a pond. Join them with arrows that point to the eater.
items.a: For example: algae → mosquito larva, algae → tadpole, mosquito larva → small fish, tadpole → small fish, small fish → kingfisher, tadpole → heron.
items.why: A web shows that most animals eat more than one thing, and are eaten by more than one thing.
items.art: An empty outline of a pond for the child to fill.

items.p: Why can there never be a food chain that starts with a tiger?
items.a: A tiger cannot make its own food. It has to eat deer, and the deer eat plants. So every chain with a tiger starts with a plant.
items.why: Food chains start with producers. Tigers are consumers.

items.p: Look at the chart. The grass in a field holds 1,000 units of food energy. About how much reaches the frogs?
items.why: Only about a tenth passes on at each step. 1,000 becomes 100 for the grasshoppers, then 10 for the frogs. Picking 250 usually means sharing the energy equally among four animals. But each animal only gets what the one before did not use up.
items.context: This chart shows a field food chain: grass, grasshoppers, frogs, snakes. At each step, only about one tenth of the food energy passes on.

chart.title: Food energy at each step of a field food chain (rounded example)

items.p: In One Hundred Grains, the grass had 100 grains. The grasshoppers got 10. The frog got ____.
items.why: 10 divided by 10 is 1. Each step keeps one tenth.
items.context: In One Hundred Grains, puffed rice grains stand for food energy. You pass them along the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake. At each step, nine out of every ten grains are used for living.

items.p: Where does most of the food energy go at each step of a food chain?
opts: It is used for living, and ends up as heat
It is stored for ever in the animal's bones
It goes back into the Sun
It is passed on to the next animal
items.why: Animals use most of their food to move, breathe, grow and stay warm. That energy leaves as heat. Picking 'passed on' is the very idea this question tests: only a small part is passed on.
items.context: In Run and Feel the Warmth, you ran on the spot for one minute and felt yourself get hot.

items.p: Why are there many deer in a forest but only a few tigers?
opts: Each tiger needs to eat lots of deer, because so little energy passes up each step
items.why: A tiger eats about 50 deer-sized animals a year. Because only about a tenth of the energy passes up each step, it takes many deer to feed one tiger. Picking 'tigers don't like each other' is partly true, since tigers live alone. But the main reason is food.

items.p: A tiger needs about 500 deer and other prey animals living in its forest, to keep it fed year after year.
items.why: True. Tiger scientists in India estimate this. A tiger eats about 50 a year, and the forest must have enough deer left to keep breeding.

items.p: In a rice field, all the frogs are caught and sold. What is most likely to happen next?
opts: Insects that eat rice increase, and the rice crop suffers
The rice grows better, because frogs eat rice
items.why: Frogs eat many insects. Without frogs, the insects that eat rice can multiply. Picking 'frogs eat rice' is a mix-up: frogs are carnivores. Picking 'snakes eat more rice' forgets that snakes are carnivores too. They will go hungry, or eat rats instead.

items.p: In the story, the posters said sparrows only eat rice. What did Lan see that the posters missed?
opts: Sparrows also eat caterpillars and other insects that eat rice
items.why: Lan saw sparrows carrying caterpillars to their chicks. So sparrows are part of a web. They eat some rice, but they also eat the insects that eat rice. Picking 'only grass' does not match what Lan saw.
items.context: In this unit's story, a girl called Lan lives in a Chinese village in 1958. Everyone is told that sparrows are pests that eat the rice, and they are chased until they die.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a producer, a consumer or a decomposer?
items.why: Algae and trees make food from light. Kingfishers and bees eat other living things. Mushrooms and soil bacteria break down dead things.

items.p: Look at the chart. Which plant was eaten most?
items.why: The hibiscus had 9 bitten leaves out of 20, more than the grass (5) or the tulsi (2). Picking tulsi usually means reading the shortest bar as the 'winner'. Here, the tallest bar means the most bites.
items.context: In the Leaf Bite Survey, you look at 20 leaves on each of three plants and count how many have bites or holes.

chart.title: Bitten leaves out of 20 on each plant (made-up results)

items.p: In the Leaf Bite Survey, why do we look at exactly 20 leaves on each plant?
opts: So the test is fair, and we can compare the plants
items.why: Imagine looking at 50 leaves on one plant and 10 on another. The first would seem to have more bites, just because we looked more. Using the same number makes it fair. Picking 'so we finish quickly' is true but not the reason.
items.context: In the Leaf Bite Survey, you look at 20 leaves on each of three plants and count how many have bites or holes.

items.p: Robert Paine kept taking starfish off one stretch of rocky shore. What happened?
opts: Mussels took over, and the number of kinds of living things fell from 15 to 8
The shore had more kinds of living things than before
The starfish grew back the next day
items.why: Starfish eat mussels. Without them, mussels covered the rocks and crowded out other living things. Picking 'more kinds' is a natural guess, since one predator was gone. But that predator kept the mussels from taking over.
items.context: Robert Paine was an American ecologist. From 1963 he tested what happens when one animal is taken out of a rocky shore.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: showed that DDT was harming birds, in Silent Spring, 1962
measured how food energy passes up the chain in a lake
counted India's vultures and found them disappearing
named keystone species after his starfish test
items.why: Each of them changed how people understand food webs. Carson and Prakash also helped save animals.

items.p: A poison like DDT can be stronger in a fish-eating bird than in the lake water.
items.why: True. Each eater keeps the poison from everything it ate, so it builds up at each step. This is called biomagnification.
items.context: In Poison Climbs the Chain, each plankton had 1 red dot. The osprey ended up with 40.

items.p: Why did India's vultures die in the 1990s and 2000s?
opts: A painkiller given to cattle stayed in the dead cattle and poisoned the vultures
They were hunted for their feathers
items.why: The painkiller diclofenac stayed in the bodies of treated cattle. Vultures that ate them died of kidney damage. Picking 'too hot' was one of the early guesses before scientists found the real cause in 2004.

items.p: When the vultures disappeared, the number of street dogs went up. Explain why, using the words 'food web'.
items.a: In the food web, vultures and dogs both ate dead cattle. With no vultures, more food was left for the dogs. So more dogs survived and had puppies.
items.why: When one eater disappears, its food goes to other eaters in the web.

items.p: Draw an energy pyramid for grass, deer and tiger. Make each layer the right size.
items.a: A wide bottom layer of grass, a smaller middle layer of deer, and a tiny top layer with one tiger.
items.why: Each step up has about a tenth of the food energy, so each layer is much smaller than the one below.
items.art: An empty triangle with two lines across it.

items.p: Most food chains have only 3 to 5 links. Which reason do scientists still argue about?
opts: Whether it is mainly because energy runs out, because long chains are wobbly, or because places are too small
items.why: Scientists have three main ideas, and they still argue about which matters most. Picking any of the others would mean the question was about something already settled.

items.p: Scientists worked out how far up the food chain humans are, on average. What did they find?
opts: About 2.2, close to a pig or an anchovy
5, the very top, above the tiger
items.why: In 2013, scientists found that humans eat mostly plants, so on average we are about 2.2. Picking 5 is what most people expect. It is how strongly we change food webs, not what we eat, that makes us powerful.
items.context: Scientists give plants the number 1, plant-eaters 2, and animals that eat plant-eaters 3, and so on, for how far up the food chain they are.

items.p: Chief Seattle really said: 'Man did not weave the web of life. He is merely a strand in it.'
items.why: False. Those words were written by a screenwriter, Ted Perry, in 1971. The idea is beautiful, but it is always worth checking who really said something.

items.p: Did bringing wolves back to Yellowstone change the shape of its rivers?
opts: Scientists still argue about how much the wolves changed the plants and rivers
No, the wolves changed nothing at all
Wolves dug new rivers with their paws
items.why: Elk numbers fell and some trees grew back, but scientists disagree about how much, and whether the rivers changed. Picking 'all scientists agree' usually comes from a popular video, which tells the story more strongly than the evidence does.

items.p: What happens to the carbon atoms in a leaf that a goat eats?
opts: They become part of the goat, or are breathed out into the air
They are destroyed inside the goat
They turn into energy and disappear
They go back into the Sun
items.why: Atoms are never destroyed. The goat builds some into its body and breathes some out. Picking 'turn into energy and disappear' mixes up atoms with energy. Energy is used up as heat. Atoms go round and round.
items.context: In Journey of a Carbon Atom, you rolled a dice to move one carbon atom between the air, a leaf, a goat, a tiger, the soil and a mushroom.

items.p: Why does life on Earth need fresh sunlight every day, but not fresh atoms?
opts: Energy is used up as heat at each step, but atoms are used again and again
Atoms come from the Sun every day
Plants only need light, not atoms
items.why: Food energy is used once and leaves as heat. Atoms are recycled by decomposers. Picking 'atoms come from the Sun every day' is a mix-up. Almost all the atoms in living things have been on Earth for billions of years.

items.p: In the Deer and Tiger Toss game, which usually comes first?
opts: The most deer, then the most tigers
The most tigers, then the most deer
Both at exactly the same time
items.why: The tigers can only increase once there are many deer to eat. So the deer peak first, and the tigers a few rounds later. Picking 'the most tigers first' would mean tigers grow without food.
items.context: In the Deer and Tiger Toss game, card tigers are dropped onto paper deer. Tigers that catch enough deer survive and have cubs. The deer that are left have babies.

items.p: Rachel Carson was attacked when she said DDT was harming birds. Why do you think some people did not want to hear it?
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: companies were making money from selling DDT. Farmers found it useful. It is hard to hear that something you rely on is causing harm.
items.why: This question links science to people. Evidence is not always welcome, and the people who bring it may need courage.

items.p: Is the tiger at the 'top' of the food chain the most powerful living thing in the forest? Give one reason for yes and one for no.
items.a: Yes: nothing hunts a grown tiger. No: the tiger depends on 500 prey animals and huge amounts of grass. If the grass fails, the tiger starves, but the grass does not need the tiger.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason for each side.

items.p: A farmer sprays a strong poison to kill insects on her crop. Next year the insects come back worse. Use the food web to explain how this could happen.
items.a: The poison also killed the frogs, spiders, birds and helpful insects that ate the crop insects. The crop insects breed faster than their predators, so they came back first, with fewer hunters.
items.why: Killing one part of a web can harm its predators more than the pest itself.

items.p: Why was what happened to India's vultures not quite the same as DDT biomagnification?
opts: One meal of a treated cow could kill a vulture, without slow build-up
Vultures are not in food webs
items.why: Biomagnification is slow build-up over many meals and many steps. Diclofenac was so harmful to vultures that a single meal could be enough. Both stories show that what an animal eats passes up the web. Picking 'not a poison' is wrong: it is a safe medicine for cattle, but deadly to vultures.

items.p: How could you test, near your home, whether lizards really come to lights because insects gather there?
items.a: For example: watch two lights at the same time on the same evening, one on and one off. Count insects and lizards at each, three times. If lizards come only to the light with many insects, that supports the idea.
items.why: A good test changes one thing, here whether the light is on, and counts carefully.
items.context: In the Tube-Light Food Chain, you counted insects and house lizards by an outside light after dark.

items.p: Which web is likely to be harder to break?
opts: A web where each animal eats many different things
A web where each animal eats only one thing
A web with only two living things
They are all equally hard to break
items.why: If an animal has many foods, losing one food is not a disaster. Picking 'only one thing' is the opposite: then losing one food means starving. Scientists still argue about very big, complicated webs, but this simple idea holds well.

items.p: Should people try to get rid of animals they call pests, like rats or crows? Give your opinion with one reason for and one against.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: for, rats eat stored grain and spread disease. Against, rats are food for owls and snakes, and crows clean up waste. Removing them may cause new problems.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer uses the food web to think about what else would change.

items.p: Draw the food web from the story: rice, caterpillar, sparrow. Draw every arrow Lan drew.
items.a: Three arrows: rice → sparrow, rice → caterpillar, caterpillar → sparrow.
items.why: The sparrow has two arrows going into it. It eats rice, and it eats the caterpillars that eat rice.
items.context: In this unit's story, a girl called Lan draws arrows between a rice plant, a caterpillar and a sparrow in her school notebook.

items.p: Some places put gambusia fish in ponds to eat mosquito larvae. Later, the fish also ate the eggs of local fish and frogs. What does this show?
opts: Adding an animal to a web can change more than you planned
Mosquitoes are not in food webs
items.why: Every animal eats more than one thing, so a new animal touches many threads in the web. Picking 'fish never eat larvae' is wrong: gambusia do eat them. The problem is what else they eat.

experiments.title: Sugar, Salt or Roti? What do ants choose?
experiments.question: Which food do ants come to most: sugar, salt, roti or nothing at all?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which square will have the most ants after 30 minutes? Which will have none? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason down.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the food. Use the same size of paper square, the same amount of each food, the same distance from the ants, and the same start time. One square has no food at all, so you can see how many ants wander onto a square by chance. Count all four squares at the same moment.

materials.item: 4 small squares of paper, each about as big as a matchbox
half a teaspoon of sugar, half a teaspoon of salt, and a piece of roti or bread the size of your thumbnail
a place where you have seen ants, such as a kitchen corner, a balcony, a doorstep or the base of a tree
a clock or a phone timer, a pencil and the results table
a magnifying glass (if you have one)

experiments.safety: Some ants bite, especially big red ants. Watch them, but don't touch them. Wipe the place with soapy water afterwards, so the ants don't keep coming back. Don't do this next to food jars or the baby's things.

schedule.what: Guess, set out four squares, then count the ants on each after 10, 20 and 30 minutes. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each square, as tall as the number of ants after 30 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the sugar, salt and roti. 2. Ask which one ants will choose, and why. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Ants are consumers. They can't make their own food, so they go looking for it. Which of these do you think they will go to most? Which will they ignore?
flow.kid: Ants can't make their own food. They must find it. Will they go to the sugar, the salt or the roti? Write your guess.

ask.q: Why did you choose that one?
good: I have seen ants on sugar.
Roti is food, but salt is not really food.

flow.context: This is the first step of the ant food test. You find out which food ants choose, by putting four squares near their path and counting.

flow.do: 1. Find a place where you have seen ants. 2. Lay the 4 squares in a row, about one hand-width apart and about two hand-widths from the ants' path. 3. Put sugar on one, salt on the next, roti on the third, and nothing on the fourth. 4. Note the time.
flow.say: Let's put them all the same distance from the ants. This empty square tells us how many ants walk onto a square just by chance.
flow.kid: Lay 4 squares in a row, one hand apart. Put sugar, salt and roti on three. Leave one empty. Note the time.
flow.parent: If you have not seen ants anywhere, leave a pinch of sugar in a balcony corner or by the kitchen door the evening before. Ants usually find it by morning, and then you know where to set up. You can also try the base of a tree, a crack near the kitchen door, or a balcony corner. Ants are busiest in warm weather and in the late afternoon. In the cold months there may be fewer.

flow.do: 1. After 10 minutes, count the ants on each square and write the numbers down. 2. Count again at 20 minutes and at 30 minutes. 3. In between, read the story or play a game nearby.
flow.say: Time to count. Count only the ants that are on the paper. If there are too many, count the ones touching the food.
flow.kid: After 10 minutes, count the ants on each square. Write the numbers. Count again at 20 and 30 minutes.
flow.parent: Usually the sugar square fills up with ants, and the roti gets some. The salt and empty squares get almost none. Sometimes no ants come at all in 15 minutes. Then move the squares closer to a trail you can see, and start the clock again. If ants come to every square equally, they may just be crossing; count only the ants that stop at the food. Now and then a few ants visit the salt. Ants need a little salt, as we do, but salt gives them no energy. Some tiny ants also love oily or meaty crumbs. That is a real result: those ants are omnivores.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Draw a bar chart together, with one bar for each square, using the 30-minute numbers.
flow.say: Each square gets one bar. The taller the bar, the more ants came to that food.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each square. Make it as tall as the number of ants at 30 minutes.

check.q: Ants came to the sugar and the roti, but not to the salt. What do sugar and roti have in common?
check.why: Sugar is made from sugarcane, a plant. Roti is made from wheat, a plant. So both carry food energy that a plant made from sunlight. Salt comes from the sea or from rocks. It was never made by a living thing, so it gives ants no energy. Picking 'both are white' means looking at the colour, which is true of sugar and salt, but not of what ants need.

chart.title: Made-up example: ants on each square after 30 minutes
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: ants choose food that came from plants, most of all sugar. What I saw: 23 ants on the sugar and 7 on the roti after 30 minutes, but none on the salt. Why: sugar and roti carry energy that plants made from sunlight, and salt has no energy for ants. So the ants are part of a food chain: sugarcane → ant.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you put sugar, salt, roti and an empty square near some ants, and count which one they come to. It shows that ants, like all consumers, need food first made by a plant.

experiments.title: Leaf Bite Survey: who is eating our plants?
experiments.question: Which plant near us gets eaten the most? And who is eating it?
experiments.predict: Look at three plants without touching them. Guess which one has the most leaves with bites or holes in them, and say why you think so. Then guess what is doing the biting.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, look at the same number of leaves on each plant: 20. Take them in order along a stem, not just the ones that look interesting. Count a leaf as bitten if it has any hole, chewed edge or trail on it.

materials.item: three different plants: pots on a balcony or windowsill, or plants in a garden, a park or by the road. Tulsi, hibiscus (gudhal), money plant, curry leaf or grass all work. If you have only one or two pots, add a bunch of palak or methi from the market.
a magnifying glass (if you have one)
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: If you go outdoors, go with a grown-up. Don't touch hairy caterpillars: their hairs can make your skin itch and burn. Look at insects without picking them up. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Count bitten leaves on three plants. Hunt for the eaters, and for who eats them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart of bitten leaves for each plant. Then draw one food chain you found, starting with a plant.

flow.do: Choose three different plants with your child. Ask them to guess which has the most bitten leaves.
flow.say: Plants are producers. They make food, and lots of animals eat them. Which of these three plants do you think gets eaten the most?
flow.kid: Pick three different plants. Look, don't touch. Which one has the most bites? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Leaf Bite Survey. You count bitten leaves on three plants, then hunt for the animals that bit them.

flow.do: 1. On each plant, look at 20 leaves in a row along a stem. 2. Count how many have a hole, a chewed edge or a wiggly trail. 3. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Count 20 leaves on each plant, one after another. Any hole, chewed edge or wiggly trail counts as a bite.
flow.kid: Look at 20 leaves on each plant, one after another. Count the leaves with holes or bites. Write the number.
flow.parent: A wiggly pale line inside a leaf is a tunnel made by a tiny caterpillar living inside it, called a leaf miner. It counts. Plants with strong-smelling or bitter leaves, like tulsi and neem, often have fewer bites. That is a real result: many plants make chemicals that stop insects eating them.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: 1. Hunt for the eaters. Look under leaves, along stems and in the soil at the base. 2. Then look for animals that might eat those eaters: spiders, ants, garden lizards and birds.
flow.say: Now let's find out who did the biting. Look under the leaves. Then look for anyone who might eat the biters.
flow.kid: Who did the biting? Look under the leaves and along the stems. Then look for spiders, lizards or birds that eat the biters.
flow.parent: Many leaf-eaters hide in the day and feed at night. If you find holes but no eaters, look again after dark with a torch, or early in the morning. Snails and slugs leave shiny trails. Little black droppings on a leaf mean a caterpillar is close.

good: A bird, like a bulbul or a myna.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of bitten leaves, and one food chain from what you saw.
flow.say: Let's draw a bar for each plant. Then let's draw one real food chain from our garden.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each plant. Then draw one real chain, like hibiscus → caterpillar → bulbul.

check.q: You found a caterpillar on a hibiscus leaf, and saw a bulbul eat a caterpillar. Which food chain is right?
check.why: A food chain starts with the producer, the plant. Then each arrow points to the eater: the caterpillar eats the hibiscus, and the bulbul eats the caterpillar. Picking 'Bulbul → caterpillar → hibiscus' means the arrows are pointing at the food instead of at the eater. Picking 'Caterpillar → hibiscus' means the plant was put second, but a plant never eats a caterpillar.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the hibiscus gets eaten most, and tulsi least. What I saw: 9 of 20 hibiscus leaves had bites, but only 2 of 20 tulsi leaves. I found two caterpillars on the hibiscus. Why: caterpillars like hibiscus leaves, and tulsi smells strong, which may keep insects away.

experiments.title: The Tube-Light Food Chain
experiments.question: Do house lizards wait where their food gathers?
experiments.predict: Guess. If one outside light is left on after dark, will more insects come to it as time goes on? Will a lizard come too? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Watch the same light at three times: 15 minutes after sunset, 30 minutes later, and 30 minutes after that. Count for one full minute each time, from the same spot. If you can, also watch a second outside light that you keep switched off, so you can compare.
results_table: Insects near the light that is on
Lizards near the light that is on
Insects near the light that is off

materials.item: an outside light, a balcony light or a stairway light that you can switch on after dark
a torch, or the torch on a phone, for checking the switched-off light
a clock, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Watch from inside a closed window or from a doorway, so insects and mosquitoes don't come in. Don't touch the lizards. A grown-up should be with you outside after dark.

schedule.what: Count insects and lizards by a light three times in the evening, 30 minutes apart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the food chain you saw. Write what time the first lizard came.

flow.do: 1. Before sunset, choose an outside light you can see through a window or from a doorway. 2. Ask your child to guess what will happen when it is switched on after dark. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Tonight we'll be nature detectives at our own window. Lots of insects fly to lights at night. Who do you think comes to eat them?
flow.kid: Tonight you will watch a light after dark. Will insects come? Will anything come to eat them? Guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tube-Light Food Chain. You watch an outside light after dark, and count the insects and the house lizards that hunt them.

flow.do: 1. Switch on the light about 15 minutes after sunset. Count the insects near it for one minute, and look for lizards. 2. Count again 30 minutes later. 3. Count again 30 minutes after that. 4. Each time, shine the torch near a light that is off and count the insects there.
flow.say: Let's count for one whole minute. How many insects? Any lizards? Where are they waiting?
flow.kid: Count the insects by the light for one minute. Look for lizards. Do it again in 30 minutes, and again 30 minutes later.
flow.parent: In most Indian homes, moths, flies and small beetles gather at lights, especially in the warm and rainy months. House geckos come to hunt them. In winter there may be very few insects, so try again on a warm night. If you never see a gecko, look for spider webs near the light instead. Spiders build there for the same reason. In a flat with sealed windows, a stairway or porch light works well.

good: On the wall, near where the insects land.

flow.do: Draw the food chain you saw, starting with a plant.
flow.say: The moth grew up as a caterpillar, eating leaves. So what is the whole food chain?
flow.kid: Draw the chain. Start with a plant. The moth was a caterpillar once, eating leaves.

check.q: A gecko eats a moth by the light. The moth, when it was a caterpillar, ate leaves. Which is the full food chain?
check.why: Food chains start with the producer, the plant that made the food. The moth's body was built from leaves it ate as a caterpillar. The gecko eats the moth. Picking 'light' is a clever mistake: the light brought the moth there, but the light is not food. The moth's energy came from leaves, and the leaves' energy came from the Sun.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: lizards wait where their food gathers. What I saw: there were 3 insects at the first count, 12 at the second and 20 at the third. One lizard came at the second count, and two at the third. The light that was off had almost no insects. Why: the light attracts the insects to one place, so the lizards can catch them easily.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you watch an outside light after dark. You count the insects that gather there, and the house lizards that come to eat them.

activities.title: Spot an Eater

materials.item: a window, balcony, garden or park, and a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Watch animals from a distance.

schedule.what: Find one living thing eating, and build its food chain to four links.

activities.record: Write or draw one food chain of four links, with arrows that point to the eater.

flow.do: 1. Sit at a window, on a balcony or in a garden for 5 minutes. 2. Together, look for any living thing that is eating, or hunting. 3. Write down who is eating, and what.
flow.say: Let's be quiet and look for 5 minutes. Can you find anything eating? A bird pecking, an ant carrying, a caterpillar chewing?
flow.kid: Look quietly for 5 minutes. Find something eating. A bird pecking? An ant carrying a crumb? Write down who eats what.
flow.parent: Good things to spot are crows at a bin, and mynas or bulbuls in a tree. Look for ants carrying crumbs, a spider in its web, or a goat eating. If you are indoors with no view, look in the kitchen for ants, or at the light for a gecko.
flow.context: This is the first step of Spot an Eater. You look around you for any living thing that is eating, and then build its food chain.

flow.do: 1. Take one eater you saw. 2. Ask: what did its food eat? Go back until you reach a plant. 3. Then ask: what might eat this eater? 4. Write the chain with arrows pointing to the eater.
flow.say: The crow ate a caterpillar. What did the caterpillar eat? Leaves. And who might eat the crow? Let's write it with arrows. The arrow points to whoever does the eating.
flow.kid: Take one eater. What did its food eat? Go back to a plant. Who might eat your eater? Write it with arrows.

check.q: A crow eats a caterpillar. The caterpillar ate a mango leaf. Which way does the first arrow point?
options: From the mango leaf to the caterpillar
From the caterpillar to the mango leaf
check.why: The arrow points from the food to the eater. The food goes out of the leaf and into the caterpillar, so the arrow goes from the leaf to the caterpillar. Picking the other way usually means the arrow was drawn like a finger pointing at the food. In a food chain, it points to the mouth.

flow.do: Ask your child what is at the start of every chain you made.
flow.say: Look at the start of your chain. What is always there?
flow.kid: Look at the start of your chain. What is there? Is it always a plant?
flow.think: The plant at the start of your chain got its food from the Sun. Where did the Sun get its energy from?

activities.context: This is a short looking activity to start the unit. You find any living thing that is eating, and build its food chain back to a plant.

activities.title: One Hundred Grains: where does the food go?

materials.item: 100 grains of puffed rice (murmura), or 100 dried chana or rajma
4 small bowls or steel katoris, labelled GRASS, GRASSHOPPER, FROG and SNAKE
1 big bowl labelled USED FOR LIVING
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: If small children are nearby, use puffed rice, not hard chana, so nothing can be choked on.

schedule.what: Pass 100 grains of food along a food chain and see how few reach the snake.

activities.record: Write how many grains each animal got. Draw the four bowls as a pyramid.

flow.do: 1. Make 10 small heaps of 10 grains each. Your child can count them, or you can count while they watch. 2. Put all 10 heaps in the GRASS bowl.
flow.say: These 100 grains are all the food energy stored in the grass of one field. The grass made it from sunlight. Let's see how much reaches the snake.
flow.kid: Make 10 heaps of 10 grains. That is 100 grains. Put them all in the GRASS bowl. That is the grass's food from the Sun.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Hundred Grains. Puffed rice grains stand for food energy, passed along the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake.

flow.do: 1. Grasshoppers eat only some of the grass. The rest dies, and decomposers use it. 2. The grasshoppers use most of what they eat to hop, breathe and stay alive. Move 9 heaps into the USED FOR LIVING bowl. 3. Move the last heap of 10 grains into the GRASSHOPPER bowl. This is the food that became grasshopper body.
flow.say: Grasshoppers eat only some of the grass. The rest dies and feeds the decomposers. And the grasshoppers use most of what they eat just to live. Out of 100 grains, how many do you think become grasshopper?
flow.kid: Grasshoppers eat only some of the grass. They use most of it just to live. Put 9 heaps in USED FOR LIVING. Only 1 heap becomes grasshopper. That is 10 grains.

flow.do: 1. The grasshoppers use most of their food to hop, breathe and keep warm, and some comes out as poo. Move 9 grains into USED FOR LIVING. 2. Move 1 grain into the FROG bowl. 3. Now break that one grain into 10 crumbs. Move 9 crumbs to USED FOR LIVING, and 1 crumb to the SNAKE bowl.
flow.say: The grasshoppers use most of their food too. Only one grain in ten passes to the frog. And the frog uses most of that. The snake gets one tiny crumb.
flow.kid: The grasshoppers use 9 grains to live. The frog gets just 1 grain. Break it into 10 crumbs. The snake gets one crumb!

check.q: The field started with 100 grains of food. How much reached the snake?
options: One tiny crumb, a tenth of one grain
check.why: At each step, only about a tenth passes on. 100 becomes 10, 10 becomes 1, and 1 becomes one tenth of a grain. The rest was used for living: growing, moving, breathing, keeping warm. Picking 'about a quarter' usually means sharing the food out equally among the four. But food is not shared out. Each eater gets only what the one before it did not use up.

flow.do: Look at the USED FOR LIVING bowl. Talk about where that food really went.
flow.say: Look how full this bowl is. In real life, most of this became heat, in the grasshoppers, the frog, the snake and the decomposers. Every living thing gives off a little warmth. That warmth can never be eaten by anyone.
flow.kid: Look at the USED FOR LIVING bowl. It is almost full! Most real food energy turns into warmth. Nobody can eat warmth.
flow.think: If an eagle ate the snake, how much would the eagle get? Could anything big live above the eagle?
flow.parent: A real field has many grasshoppers, frogs and snakes, but the pattern is the same. Scientists find that usually between one twentieth and one fifth passes on, so one tenth is a good round number. This is why chains are short, and why there are so few top predators.

activities.context: This is a hands-on model with grains of puffed rice. Each grain stands for some food energy. You pass the food along a food chain and see how little reaches the end.

setup.caption: 1. Make 10 heaps of 10 grains. Put them in the GRASS bowl.

setup.caption: 2. Nine heaps are used for living. One heap goes to the grasshoppers.

activities.title: Run and Feel the Warmth

materials.item: a little space to run on the spot, and a clock

activities.safety: Run on the spot on a non-slip floor. Stop if you feel dizzy.

schedule.what: Run on the spot for a minute and feel where your food's energy goes.

activities.record: Write three ways you could tell your body was using energy: for example, hot face, fast breathing, sweat.

flow.do: 1. Feel your child's forehead and count their breaths for 15 seconds. 2. Run on the spot together, fast, for one minute.
flow.say: First, let's feel your forehead and count your breaths. Now run on the spot as fast as you can for one minute!
flow.kid: Feel your forehead. Count your breaths for 15 seconds. Now run on the spot, fast, for one whole minute!
flow.context: This is the first step of Run and Feel the Warmth. You run on the spot to feel what happens to the energy in your food.

flow.do: 1. Stop. Feel the forehead again and count the breaths again. 2. Talk about where the energy came from, and where it went.
flow.say: Feel how hot you are. Count your breaths. That heat and that movement came from your breakfast. And now the heat is leaving you, into the air.
flow.kid: Stop! Feel your forehead. Count your breaths again. That heat came from your food. Now it is going into the air.

check.q: After running, you feel hot. Where did that heat come from?
options: From the energy in the food you ate
From the sunshine on your skin
check.why: Your muscles used energy from your food to move you. Most of that energy became heat, which is why you got hot. The heat then leaves your skin and warms the air a little. Picking 'sunshine' is a sensible guess on a sunny day. But you get hot running indoors too, because the heat is made inside you.

flow.do: Link this to the food chain.
flow.say: A frog that hops all day uses up its food like you just did. When a snake eats the frog, it only gets what is left in the frog's body. The hopping and the warmth are gone for ever.
flow.kid: A frog uses its food to hop, just like you ran. When a snake eats the frog, the hops are gone. The snake gets only what is left.
flow.think: You are warm right now, even sitting still. How much of your food do you think goes into just keeping warm?
flow.parent: People, birds and other mammals use a large share of their food just to stay warm, all day and all night. Cold-blooded animals like frogs, snakes and lizards do not, so they need far less food. A snake can live for weeks on one meal. A shrew must eat almost all the time.

activities.context: This short activity lets you feel your food's energy turning into movement and heat. It shows why so little food passes up a food chain.

setup.caption: 1. Feel your forehead. Count your breaths.

setup.caption: 2. Run on the spot for one minute.

activities.title: Pull One Thread: a wool food web

materials.item: a ball of wool or string
12 role cards: Sun, grass, neem tree, grasshopper, caterpillar, chital deer, frog, bulbul, rat snake, tiger, vulture, mushroom
if you have only 2 or 3 people: chair legs, toys or water bottles to hold the extra cards

activities.safety: Pull gently. Wind the wool up afterwards so nobody trips on it.

schedule.what: Build a food web out of wool, then cut one thread and feel what moves.

activities.record: Draw the web you made. Circle the living thing that had the most threads.

flow.do: 1. Sit in a circle. 2. Give each person one or more role cards. 3. With only 2 or 3 people, tie the extra cards to chair legs, toys or bottles placed around the circle.
flow.say: Each of us is a living thing in a forest. When the wool goes from one card to another, it means 'is eaten by'.
flow.kid: Sit in a circle. Take your role cards. Put extra cards on toys or chair legs. The wool will join each food to its eater.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pull One Thread. You build a food web out of wool, with each person or toy holding a living thing.

flow.do: 1. The Sun holds the end of the wool. 2. Pass the ball from the Sun to the grass. 3. Keep passing it from each food to one of its eaters, and say each link out loud. 4. Each holder wraps the wool once round a finger, or round the toy, before passing it on. 5. Keep going until every card has at least two threads.
flow.say: The Sun to the grass. The grass to the grasshopper. The grasshopper to the frog. Who eats the frog? Keep going until everyone has at least two threads.
flow.kid: Pass the wool from food to eater. Sun to grass. Grass to grasshopper. Say each link out loud. Give everyone two threads.
flow.parent: Good links: Sun to grass and neem tree. Grass to grasshopper and chital deer. Neem tree to caterpillar and chital deer. Grasshopper to frog and bulbul. Caterpillar to bulbul and frog. Frog to rat snake. Chital deer to tiger. Any dead animal to the vulture. Any dead plant or animal to the mushroom. Mushroom back to the soil, which feeds the grass.

flow.do: 1. Pull the web gently tight. 2. Say: 'A drought kills the grass.' The grass holder lets go, or the grass toy falls over. 3. Everyone who feels a tug lets go too. 4. Count who is still holding.
flow.say: Pull it gently tight. Now a drought kills the grass. Grass, let go! Who felt the web move? If your food has gone, you let go too.
flow.kid: Pull the web tight. A drought kills the grass! Grass lets go. Did you feel a tug? Who is still holding on?

check.q: In the wool web, the grass let go. Which living thing felt it, even though it never eats grass?
options: The tiger, because the deer it eats needed the grass
Nobody, because only grass-eaters are affected
check.why: The tiger eats deer, and deer eat grass. When the grass goes, the deer go hungry, and then the tiger does too. In a web, a change travels along the threads to animals far away. Picking 'only grass-eaters' means looking at one link instead of the whole web.

flow.do: Build the web again. This time take away the vulture and the mushroom, and talk about what would happen to dead animals and plants.
flow.say: Now let's take away the vulture and the mushroom. What happens to every animal that dies? Where do the grass's new nutrients come from?
flow.kid: Now take away the vulture and the mushroom. What happens to dead animals? Who cleans up now?
flow.think: Which living thing in our web held the most threads? Is that the most important one, or just the busiest?

activities.context: In this activity you build a food web out of wool. Each person, or a toy, holds a living thing, and the wool joins each food to its eater. Then you take one living thing away and feel what moves.

setup.caption: 2. Pass the wool from each food to its eater.

activities.title: Poison Climbs the Chain

materials.item: 40 small squares of paper, to be the plankton (tiny water plants and animals)
40 red beads, red bindis or small red paper dots, to be the poison
8 paper cups or small bowls for small fish, 2 for big fish, and 1 for an osprey (a fish-eating bird)

activities.safety: Keep beads away from babies and toddlers.

schedule.what: Pass red poison dots up a food chain and count how many reach the bird.

activities.record: Write how many red dots each animal had. Draw the chain with the number of dots beside each animal.

flow.do: 1. Spread the 40 paper plankton on the floor. 2. Put one red dot on each. 3. Line up the 8 small-fish cups, the 2 big-fish cups and the 1 osprey cup.
flow.say: A chemical called DDT was sprayed to kill insects. A little washed into a lake. Each tiny water creature took in a tiny bit. Each red dot is one tiny bit of poison.
flow.kid: Spread out 40 paper plankton. Put one red dot on each. Each dot is a tiny bit of poison from the lake.
flow.context: This is the first step of Poison Climbs the Chain. Red dots stand for a poison called DDT, and you pass them up a food chain from plankton to fish to a bird.

flow.do: 1. Each small fish eats 5 plankton. Put 5 plankton, with their dots, into each small-fish cup. 2. Each big fish eats 4 small fish. Empty 4 small-fish cups into each big-fish cup. 3. The osprey eats both big fish. Empty both into the osprey cup. 4. Count the red dots at each step.
flow.say: The poison doesn't wash out of their bodies. So each eater keeps the poison from everything it ate. Let's count the dots.
flow.kid: Each small fish eats 5 plankton. Each big fish eats 4 small fish. The osprey eats both big fish. Count the dots each time!

check.q: Each plankton had 1 red dot. How many dots did the osprey end up with?
check.why: Each small fish ate 5 plankton, so it had 5 dots. Each big fish ate 4 small fish, so it had 20 dots. The osprey ate both big fish, so it had 40 dots. The poison stayed in each body and was passed up. Picking '1 dot' means thinking the bird only gets as much as one plankton. But the bird ate everything the fish ate.

flow.do: Tell the real story of DDT and Rachel Carson.
flow.say: In real lakes, DDT in fish-eating birds became many thousands of times stronger than in the water. It made their eggshells so thin that they broke. A scientist called Rachel Carson told the world in 1962, in a book called Silent Spring. People with money to lose attacked her. But she was right, and DDT was banned for farming in many countries.
flow.kid: In real lakes, the birds at the top got the most DDT. Their eggshells got thin and broke. Rachel Carson told the world in 1962.

flow.do: Talk about how this is different from what happened to India's vultures.
flow.say: India's vultures were poisoned by a cattle medicine, diclofenac. That was different. A vulture didn't need to build it up slowly. One meal from a treated cow could kill it. But both stories show the same thing. What an animal eats passes up the food web.
flow.kid: India's vultures were poisoned by a cow medicine. One meal could kill them. What an animal eats passes up the web.
flow.think: Is there anything we put into the world that ends up coming back to us through our food?

activities.context: This activity shows how some poisons build up as they go up a food chain. You pass red dots from tiny water creatures to small fish, to big fish, to a fish-eating bird.

activities.title: Journey of a Carbon Atom (a dice game)

materials.item: 6 sheets of paper, labelled AIR, LEAF, GOAT, TIGER, SOIL and MUSHROOM, spread around a room
one dice and one small black button or stone, which is the carbon atom
a pencil and paper to write the journey

activities.safety: Walk between the sheets, don't run on a slippery floor.

schedule.what: Roll a dice to move a carbon atom around a food web, and write its journey.

activities.record: Write the atom's whole journey with arrows. Count how many times it came back to the AIR.

flow.do: 1. Put the six sheets around the room. 2. Put the button on AIR. 3. Explain that the button is one carbon atom, the kind every living thing is built from.
flow.say: This button is one carbon atom. Every leaf, goat, tiger and you are built of atoms like it. It starts in the air. Let's see where it travels.
flow.kid: This button is a carbon atom. You are built from atoms like it. It starts in the AIR. Where will it go?
flow.context: This is the first step of Journey of a Carbon Atom. You roll a dice to move one atom from the air, through living things, and back again.

flow.do: Roll the dice at each sheet and move the atom. At AIR: 1 to 4, a leaf takes it in (go to LEAF). 5 or 6, stay in the air. At LEAF: 1 to 3, a goat eats it (GOAT). 4 to 6, the leaf falls and rots (SOIL). At GOAT: 1 or 2, a tiger eats the goat (TIGER). 3 to 6, the goat breathes it out (AIR). At TIGER: 1 to 4, the tiger breathes it out (AIR). 5 or 6, the tiger dies (SOIL). At SOIL: 1 to 6, a mushroom eats it (MUSHROOM). At MUSHROOM: 1 to 6, it is breathed out (AIR). Write each move down. Play 15 moves.
flow.say: Roll the dice and read what happens. Walk the atom to its next home. Let's write down each move.
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Read what happens. Carry the atom to its next home. Write it down. Do 15 moves.
flow.parent: The real numbers are different, and much slower: an atom may stay in a tree for a hundred years. But the idea is right. Atoms go round and round between air, plants, animals, soil and decomposers, and are never used up.

flow.do: Read the journey out loud together.
flow.say: Did the atom ever stop for good? Did it ever get used up? Food energy gets used up at every step. But the atoms just keep going round.
flow.kid: Read your atom's journey. Did it ever get used up? Food energy gets used up. Atoms just keep going round.

check.q: What happens to the carbon atoms in a tiger's body after it dies?
options: Decomposers break the body down, and the atoms go back to the soil and air
They stay in the bones for ever
check.why: Atoms are never destroyed. Beetles, fungi and bacteria eat the tiger's body. They breathe out some of its carbon into the air, and some goes into the soil. A plant can then use it again. Picking 'disappear' mixes up atoms with energy. Energy is used up as heat. Atoms are not.

flow.think: Could one of the atoms in your hand once have been inside a tiger, or a dinosaur?

activities.context: This is a dice game. You move one carbon atom around six homes: the air, a leaf, a goat, a tiger, the soil and a mushroom. It shows that atoms go round and round, while food energy is used up.

setup.caption: 1. Put six homes around the room. The atom starts in the AIR.

setup.art: A child rolling a dice beside the leaf sheet, holding the black button.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the dice. Move the atom to its next home.

setup.caption: 3. Write down the whole journey.

projects.title: Our Street's Food Web

materials.item: a big sheet of chart paper, or four A4 sheets taped together
colour pencils or crayons, and a notebook
a magnifying glass, and binoculars if you have them

projects.safety: Watch animals from a distance. Go outdoors with a grown-up. Don't feed wild animals or touch dead ones.

schedule.what: Watch for 10 minutes at one spot near home. Write down every living thing you see, and anything you see eating.
Watch at the same spot at a different time of day. Add new living things and new eating.
Watch after dark, at a light or with a torch, with a grown-up. Add night animals.
Look for clean-up crews: ants on a dead insect, mould, mushrooms, crows at a bin. Add them.
Draw the whole food web on the big sheet. Colour each kind of living thing. Find the busiest one. Show it to the family.

projects.record: The finished food web chart, with every arrow pointing to the eater, and a list of what you saw each day.

flow.do: 1. Choose one spot near home: a window, a balcony, a garden, a park bench or a tree by the road. 2. Watch for 10 minutes. 3. Write down every living thing you see, and anything eating.
flow.say: For five days we will be ecologists, scientists who study who lives where and who eats whom. Let's start a list of every living thing at our spot.
flow.kid: You are an ecologist for five days! Watch your spot for 10 minutes. Write every living thing you see. Did anything eat?
flow.context: This is the first step of the five-day food web project. Each day you watch one spot near home, and on the last day you draw its whole food web.

flow.do: Watch the same spot at a different time, for example early morning if you went in the afternoon. Add new living things and new eating.
flow.say: Are the same animals here now? Who comes in the morning but not the afternoon?
flow.kid: Watch the same spot at a new time. Who is new? Who has gone? Add them to your list.

flow.do: After dark, with a grown-up, look at an outside light or shine a torch on a wall or plant. Add night animals: moths, geckos, spiders, bats, frogs.
flow.say: Many animals only come out at night. Let's look for the night shift.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, look at a light after dark. Who comes at night? Moths? Lizards? Bats? Add them.

flow.do: Look for the clean-up crew. Find ants carrying a dead insect, mould on fallen fruit, or mushrooms. Look for crows at a bin, and earthworms under a pot.
flow.say: Who eats the dead things around here? Let's find the clean-up crew.
flow.kid: Find the clean-up crew. Ants on a dead insect? Mushrooms? Crows at a bin? Earthworms under a pot? Add them.

flow.do: 1. Draw each living thing on the big sheet, with plants at the bottom. 2. Draw an arrow from each food to its eater. 3. Colour producers green, herbivores yellow, carnivores red, omnivores orange and the clean-up crew brown. 4. Find the living thing with the most arrows. 5. Show the web to the family.
flow.say: Plants go at the bottom. Every arrow goes from the food to the eater. Which living thing has the most arrows touching it?
flow.kid: Draw everything you saw. Plants at the bottom. Arrows point to the eater. Colour them. Who has the most arrows?

check.q: On your street's food web, the crow has the most arrows. What does that tell you?
options: The crow eats many different things and is linked to many living things
The crow is the biggest animal
check.why: Each arrow is one 'is eaten by' link. A crow eats insects, roti, fruit, frogs, eggs and dead animals, so it has many arrows. Omnivores often have the most. Picking 'the biggest' mixes up size with links. A cow is bigger than a crow, but eats only plants, so it has fewer arrows.

flow.think: Where did you put yourself on the web? What do you eat that came from your street?

projects.context: In this five-day project, you watch one spot near your home each day, and list who lives there and who eats whom. On the last day, you draw your street's own food web.

challenges.title: Mosquito Trouble: fix it with the food web
challenges.problem: Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water. Their young, called larvae, live in the water for about a week before they fly. A society near you has lots of mosquitoes. Find ways to cut them down using what you know about food webs, not poison sprays.
constraints: No poison sprays: they also kill frogs, dragonflies and birds that eat mosquitoes.
Your ideas must be cheap and safe for children and pets.
Check your own home first, with a grown-up.
general: Empty any still water every week: cooler trays, flower-pot plates, old tyres, buckets and coconut shells. With no water, there are no larvae.
Cover water tanks and drums tightly.
In ponds and big tanks that cannot be emptied, health workers in many Indian towns add small fish, such as guppies, which eat mosquito larvae.
creative: Make a pond friendly for dragonflies. Their young live in water and eat mosquito larvae, and the grown dragonflies catch mosquitoes in the air.
Leave a safe, shady corner for frogs and toads. Tadpoles and frogs eat many insects.
Plant shrubs and trees that bring insect-eating birds, like bee-eaters, drongos and swallows.
challenges.your_turn: Draw a plan for your home or street. Show where water collects, which you will empty, and which eaters you will invite. Then check again after one week.

flow.do: 1. With a torch, check your home with your child for still water: cooler trays, flower-pot plates, buckets, the fridge drip tray. 2. Look closely for tiny wriggling larvae. 3. Tip the water into a drain or a plant pot.
flow.say: Let's be mosquito detectives. Where in our home does water sit still for days? Look closely for tiny wrigglers.
flow.kid: With a grown-up, hunt for still water at home. Look for tiny wriggling larvae. Then tip the water into a drain.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Mosquito Trouble challenge. You find where mosquitoes grow in your home, then plan how to cut them down using the food web.

flow.do: Draw the mosquito's food web together: who it eats, and who eats it.
flow.say: Mosquito larvae eat tiny algae and bacteria in the water. Who eats mosquito larvae? Who eats grown mosquitoes?
flow.kid: Draw the mosquito's web. What do the larvae eat? Who eats the larvae? Who eats the grown mosquitoes?

check.q: Why are poison sprays not the best way to stop mosquitoes?
options: They also kill the frogs, fish and dragonflies that eat mosquitoes
check.why: Sprays kill many insects and can harm frogs and fish. That takes away the mosquito's predators. Mosquitoes breed fast, so they can come back before their predators do. Picking 'mosquitoes like the smell' is a guess with no evidence. The real problem is what the spray does to the rest of the web.

flow.say: Mosquitoes grow from egg to flying in about a week. So we check every week.
flow.kid: Mosquitoes grow up in about a week. Put a reminder to check again next week.
flow.think: Some places brought in a fish called gambusia to eat mosquito larvae. It then ate the eggs of local fish and frogs too. How can a helper become a problem?

challenges.title: Room for a Tiger
challenges.problem: Your job is to design a forest that can feed a family of 4 tigers, year after year. Each tiger needs about 500 deer and other prey animals alive in its forest. In our made-up forest, one square of land, 1 kilometre on each side, has grass and leaves for about 20 deer.
constraints: Each square of paper is 1 square kilometre of forest.
Every tiger also needs water, thick bushes to hide its cubs, and a way to reach other forests.
People live nearby, and their farms and roads must stay safe.
materials: about 100 small paper squares (or a sheet of squared paper)
a calculator or paper for working
general: Work out the deer first: 4 tigers × 500 prey = 2,000 prey animals.
Then the land: 2,000 ÷ 20 = 100 squares of forest.
Protect one large forest, with water holes and thick cover.
creative: Join forests with corridors, strips of trees where tigers can walk safely from one forest to the next, so young tigers can find a home.
Build animal underpasses under roads. India has built some under a highway near Pench Tiger Reserve.
Help nearby villages with fences, insurance for lost cattle, or jobs as forest guides, so people and tigers can share the land.
challenges.your_turn: Lay out your own tiger forest with paper squares. Mark water, cover, villages and corridors. Explain why your forest will still feed the tigers in ten years.

flow.do: Work out together how many prey animals and how many squares of forest the 4 tigers need.
flow.say: Each tiger needs about 500 prey animals in its forest. How many for 4 tigers? And if each square holds 20 deer, how many squares do we need?
flow.kid: Each tiger needs 500 prey animals. How many for 4 tigers? Each square holds 20 deer. How many squares do you need?

check.q: 4 tigers need 2,000 prey animals. Each square of forest holds 20. How many squares are needed?
check.why: 2,000 divided by 20 is 100. You can check: 100 × 20 = 2,000. Picking 40 usually comes from multiplying 2 × 20 instead of dividing. Picking 2,000 forgets that each square holds many deer.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Room for a Tiger challenge. You work out how much forest a family of tigers needs, using the one-tenth rule of food chains.

flow.do: 1. Lay out 100 paper squares as a forest on the floor. 2. Draw water holes, thick bushes, villages, farms and roads. 3. Add corridors to other forests.
flow.say: Now let's build it. Where will the tigers drink? Where will the cubs hide? Where do people live?
flow.kid: Lay out your 100 squares. Draw water, bushes, villages and roads. Add a corridor to another forest.
flow.parent: 100 squares of 1 kilometre is about the size of a city like Chandigarh. Real tiger reserves in India are usually bigger: many are between 500 and 3,000 square kilometres, including the parts where people live.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together. Then your child explains their forest.
flow.say: Here are the usual ways, and some creative ones. Tell me why your forest will still feed the tigers in ten years.
flow.kid: Read the usual and creative ideas. Then explain your forest. Will it still feed the tigers in ten years?
flow.think: A tiger at the top of the chain needs a whole forest of deer and grass. Who does the tiger depend on most?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You work out how much forest a family of tigers needs, using the one-tenth rule of food chains, and then design that forest.

quiz.p: In a food chain, what does the arrow mean?
quiz.why: Grass → goat means the grass is eaten by the goat. The arrow shows which way the food goes. Picking 'eats' is the common mix-up: it reads the arrow backwards, as if it pointed at the food.

quiz.p: What is at the start of almost every food chain?
quiz.why: Plants and algae make food from sunlight. Every other living thing eats food that a plant made first. Picking 'a decomposer' is a clever guess, since decomposers feed the soil. But decomposers cannot make food from light.

quiz.p: Which is a correct food chain?
opts: Algae → mosquito larva → small fish → kingfisher
Kingfisher → small fish → mosquito larva → algae
Small fish → algae → kingfisher → mosquito larva
quiz.why: The chain starts with the producer, algae, and each arrow points to the eater. Picking the second one means the chain is in reverse, with the arrows pointing at the food.

quiz.p: A crow eats roti, insects, fruit and dead animals. What is the crow?
quiz.why: An omnivore eats both plants and animals. Picking 'herbivore' means the roti and fruit were counted, but not the insects and dead animals.

quiz.p: Which living thing breaks down dead plants and animals into soil?
opts: A mushroom, which is a decomposer
A tiger, which is a predator
A mango tree, which is a producer
quiz.why: Mushrooms and other fungi, and bacteria, are decomposers. Picking the mango tree usually means that anything growing from the soil is thought to be feeding it. But trees take from the soil. Decomposers give back to it.

quiz.p: All the frogs in a rice field disappear. What happens to the insects that frogs eat?
quiz.why: With fewer frogs, fewer insects are eaten, so they usually increase. Picking 'they all die' means thinking everything in a chain goes when one link goes. But the insects did not need the frogs. The frogs needed the insects.

quiz.p: Why is a food web harder to break than a single food chain?
opts: Animals can switch to other foods when one runs out
quiz.why: In a web, most animals have several foods. If one food runs out, they can eat another. Picking 'bigger animals' mixes up size with links.

quiz.p: In One Hundred Grains, the grass had 100 grains. How many reached the frog?
quiz.why: The grasshoppers got one tenth of 100, which is 10. The frog got one tenth of 10, which is 1. Picking 10 stops one step too early. Picking 25 shares the grains out equally, which is not how food passes along.
quiz.context: In One Hundred Grains, puffed rice grains stand for food energy. You pass them along the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake. At each step, nine out of every ten grains are used for living.

quiz.p: Why are there so few tigers compared to deer?
opts: Only a small part of the food energy passes up each step, so each tiger needs many deer
quiz.why: A tiger needs about 50 deer-sized animals a year, and a forest of about 500 prey animals to keep going. Picking 'deer eat tigers' has the chain the wrong way round.

quiz.why: The empty square is for comparing. It had 1 ant, while the sugar had 23. So the sugar really attracted the ants. Picking 'the test went wrong' misses why we added the empty square on purpose.

quiz.p: To make the Leaf Bite Survey fair, what must be the same for every plant?

quiz.why: Looking at 20 leaves on every plant lets us compare them fairly. Picking 'colour' changes nothing about how we count.
quiz.context: In the Leaf Bite Survey, you look at 20 leaves on each of three plants and count how many have bites or holes.

quiz.p: DDT was sprayed on insects and washed into a lake. Where did it become strongest?
opts: In the fish-eating birds at the top
quiz.why: Each eater keeps the poison from everything it ate, so it builds up at each step. Picking 'the water' is a natural guess, because that is where it went first. But there it was most spread out.
quiz.context: In Poison Climbs the Chain, each plankton had one red dot of poison, and you passed them up to small fish, big fish and an osprey.

quiz.p: What nearly wiped out India's vultures?
opts: A painkiller given to cattle, diclofenac
quiz.why: Vultures ate dead cattle that had been treated with diclofenac, and it destroyed their kidneys. India banned it for animals in 2006. Picking 'too many tigers' is a guess that tigers hunt vultures. They don't.

quiz.p: Do scientists all agree that wolves changed the rivers of Yellowstone?
opts: No, they still argue about how big the effect was
Yes, the wolves dug new rivers
quiz.why: Some scientists found trees growing back, and others found the effect much smaller. Picking 'all agree' usually comes from a popular video that tells the story more strongly than the evidence.

quiz.p: What happens to atoms and energy as food passes along a food chain?
opts: The atoms go round and round, but the energy is used up as heat
Both go round and round for ever
quiz.why: Decomposers return atoms to the soil and air, to be used again. Energy leaves as heat and does not come back, so life needs new sunlight every day. Picking 'both go round' misses why plants must keep catching light.

applications: Tiger reserves, like those set up under Project Tiger from 1973, protect whole food webs: grass, deer and tigers together.
Farmers use predators instead of poison: ladybirds eat aphids, and owls and snakes eat rats in the fields.
Health workers in many Indian towns put small fish in ponds and tanks to eat mosquito larvae.
Vulture breeding centres in India, such as the one at Pinjore in Haryana, raise vultures to release back into the wild.
Scientists test new medicines for farm animals to make sure they are safe for scavengers, like meloxicam for vultures.
Fishing rules limit how many fish are caught, so that sea food webs don't collapse.
Food advice tells people to eat big sea fish, like shark and swordfish, only sometimes, because mercury builds up in them.
Wildlife corridors and road underpasses let tigers and elephants move between forests.
Knowing the one-tenth rule helps planners work out how many people a piece of farmland can feed.
Composting kitchen waste uses decomposers to turn the end of food chains into soil for new plants.
Bird-watchers and citizen scientists count birds each year, which shows when part of a food web is in trouble.
Fish farmers and pond owners balance algae, fish and water plants so that the pond stays healthy.

open_questions.q: Why are food chains so short?
open_questions.why_open: Three main ideas compete: energy running out, long chains being wobbly, and places being too small. Experiments support each in different places.

open_questions.q: How much can one predator change a whole place?
open_questions.why_open: In some places, like Paine's rocky shore, the effect is huge. In others, like Yellowstone, scientists still argue about how big it was.

open_questions.q: Do webs with more kinds of living things stay steadier?
open_questions.why_open: Some experiments say yes. Some maths says very complicated webs can be less steady. Both may be right in different situations.

open_questions.q: How many links are there in a real food web?
open_questions.why_open: Most links involve tiny living things, like microbes and parasites, that are hard to see and count. When scientists counted parasites in some marsh food webs, they found they were part of most of the links.
Some vultures raised in breeding centres have been released, and diclofenac is banned for animals. But other cattle painkillers may also harm vultures, and numbers are still very low.

open_questions.q: How will a warming world change food webs?
open_questions.why_open: Plants, insects and birds are shifting the times they flower, hatch and nest. If a bird's chicks hatch after the caterpillars have gone, the chain breaks. Scientists are studying how often this happens.

open_questions.q: Could there be food webs on other worlds?
open_questions.why_open: Moons like Europa and Enceladus may have oceans under their ice. If life exists there, its food chains would have to start with chemicals, not sunlight. Nobody knows yet.

maths.problem: In One Hundred Grains, the grass had 100 grains. At each step, only one tenth passes on. How many grains does each animal get: grasshopper, frog, snake?
maths.answer: Grasshopper 10, frog 1, snake one tenth of a grain.
maths.explain: One tenth of 100 is 100 divided by 10, which is 10. One tenth of 10 is 10 divided by 10, which is 1. One tenth of 1 is a crumb, one tenth of a grain. You can check: 10 groups of 10 make 100.
maths.context: In One Hundred Grains, puffed rice grains stand for food energy. You pass them along the chain grass, grasshopper, frog, snake. At each step, nine out of every ten grains are used for living.
maths.why_maths: The one-tenth rule is a division. Dividing by 10 at each step shows, in numbers, why food runs out so fast as it goes up a chain.

maths.problem: A tiger eats about one deer-sized animal every week. There are 52 weeks in a year. About how many does it eat in a year? How many would a family of 3 tigers eat?
maths.answer: About 52 in a year for one tiger, and 156 for three tigers.
maths.explain: One a week for 52 weeks is 52 × 1 = 52. For three tigers, it is 52 + 52 + 52, which is 3 × 52 = 156. To work out 3 × 52: 3 × 50 = 150, and 3 × 2 = 6. 150 + 6 = 156.
maths.context: Tigers are top predators. Because so little food energy passes up a food chain, each tiger needs to eat many deer every year.

show.art: A tiger with a calendar showing 52 weeks, one small deer drawn on each week.

maths.why_maths: Multiplying one meal a week by 52 weeks turns 'tigers eat a lot' into a real number. That number tells us how big a forest a tiger needs.

maths.problem: In the ant test, these are the ants counted after 30 minutes: sugar 23, roti 7, salt 0, nothing 1. Draw a bar chart. How many more ants came to the sugar than to the roti? How many ants were there altogether?
maths.answer: 16 more ants came to the sugar. There were 31 ants altogether. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each square, as tall as its number. To find how many more: 23 take away 7 is 16. To find the total: 23 + 7 + 0 + 1 = 31.
maths.context: In the ant test, you put four paper squares near some ants: one with sugar, one with salt, one with a piece of roti, and one with nothing. Then you count the ants on each.

maths.why_maths: A list of four numbers is hard to compare at a glance. A bar chart shows straight away which food the ants chose, and subtracting tells us by how much.

maths.problem: In Poison Climbs the Chain, each of 40 plankton had 1 red dot. Each small fish ate 5 plankton. Each big fish ate 4 small fish. The osprey ate 2 big fish. How many dots did each small fish, each big fish and the osprey have?
maths.answer: Each small fish had 5 dots, each big fish 20 dots, and the osprey 40 dots.
maths.explain: A small fish ate 5 plankton with 1 dot each: 5 × 1 = 5. A big fish ate 4 small fish with 5 dots each: 4 × 5 = 20. The osprey ate 2 big fish with 20 dots each: 2 × 20 = 40. So the osprey had 40 times as much poison as one plankton.
maths.context: In Poison Climbs the Chain, red dots stand for a poison called DDT. Each eater keeps the poison from everything it ate.

answer_chart.title: Red poison dots at each step

maths.why_maths: Multiplying at each step shows how a tiny bit of poison can become a dangerous amount at the top of a food chain.

maths.problem: Look at your Deer and Tiger Toss record. In the example, the deer were 6, 10, 16, 24, 28, 36 in the first six rounds. By how much did the deer go up each round? In which round did they go up the most?
maths.answer: They went up by 4, 6, 8, 4 and 8. The biggest rise was 8, from round 3 to round 4, and again from round 5 to round 6.
maths.explain: Take each number away from the next. 10 − 6 = 4. 16 − 10 = 6. 24 − 16 = 8. 28 − 24 = 4. 36 − 28 = 8. The rise slowed down between rounds 4 and 5, because more tigers were eating deer by then.
maths.context: In the Deer and Tiger Toss game, card tigers are dropped onto paper deer. Each round, the deer that are left have babies, and the tigers that ate enough survive.

maths.why_maths: Finding the difference between each number and the next shows how fast the deer are growing, and when the tigers start to slow them down.
