roots.context: We have been learning who eats whom, and how food passes from plant to animal to animal. Now we ask what that passing tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In One Hundred Grains, only 1 grain of every 100 reached the frog. Each eater uses most of its food just to stay alive, and that energy leaves as heat. So a field of grass can feed many grasshoppers, fewer frogs and hardly any snakes. How many hunters can live at the top depends on how much plant food grows at the bottom.
deep_truth.habit: We picture the animal at the top of a food chain as the strongest, the king. In numbers, the top holds the fewest animals, and each one depends on everything below it.
deep_truth.evidence: In One Hundred Grains, 100 grains became 10, then 1. Raymond Lindeman measured the same steep drop in a real lake, published in 1942. Tiger scientists in India estimate that one tiger needs about 500 deer and other prey alive in its forest.

three.who_am_i: Your body is built from the food you ate. That food was built by plants, using sunlight.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing must eat, or make its own food from light. When it dies, its body becomes food for others.
three.what_is_this_world: Living things are linked by who eats whom. When India's vultures disappeared, street dogs grew in number, and more people caught rabies.

roots.thread: All the energy in a food web comes from one source, the Sun. Plants catch it, and it passes into grass, grasshopper, frog and snake. At every step most of it leaves as heat, so a web can only be a few steps tall. The atoms are passed on too, from body to body and back to the soil and air, and they are used again and again. So the grass, the tiger and you run on the same sunlight, and are built from atoms that have passed between you.

teachings.teaching: Living beings come from food. Food comes from rain, and rain comes from yajna, an offering. The Gita calls this a wheel that has been set turning, and says that whoever takes from it without giving back lives in vain.
teachings.link: The Gita describes a turning chain that feeds every living being. A food web is a real chain like that. Sunlight and rain grow plants, plants feed animals, and every dead body feeds the soil that grows new plants.

teachings.source: The Lakota phrase Mitákuye Oyás'iŋ, 'all my relatives', from the Lakota people of North America
teachings.teaching: Lakota people say these words to mean that every living thing, the animals, plants, rivers and stones, is a relative.
teachings.link: In a food web, the grass, the deer and the tiger are joined so closely that harming one harms the others, like a family.

teachings.teaching: The way of heaven takes from what has too much and gives to what has too little.
teachings.link: In Deer and Tiger Toss, when deer are many, tigers eat well and grow in number. Then the deer fall, the tigers go hungry and the deer recover. Scientists still argue about whether nature truly keeps a balance.

science.text: The atoms in living things are used again and again by plants, animals and decomposers. The energy passes through only once, and leaves as heat.
Places with more kinds of living things, and more links between them, often recover better after a drought or a disease. Scientists still argue about when this is true.

other_view.who: Daniel Botkin, an American ecologist, and many ecologists today
other_view.view: There is no fixed balance or plan in nature. Food webs are shaped by hunger, chance and change, and they shift all the time. On this view, energy and eating explain food chains fully, without any idea of oneness.

practice.title: The breath you share
practice.say: Let's sit still and close our eyes. Breathe in slowly. Now breathe out slowly onto your palm and feel it, warm. In that breath are carbon atoms from the food you ate today. A tree outside may take some of them in this afternoon. Breathe in again. Some of the oxygen you breathe in was given out by plants. Let's do three more slow breaths, giving and taking.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Breathe out slowly onto your hand. Feel it, warm. Your breath carries carbon from your breakfast to the trees. Breathe in. Some of that air was given out by plants. Do three more slow breaths.

playtest: Every activity was walked through as if done at home. The ant test (e1) needs a spot where ants already walk. It says what to do if none come in 15 minutes, and that results vary with the ant kind and season. The Leaf Bite Survey (e2) works with any three plants. Strong-smelling plants like tulsi often have few bites, which is a real result. The Tube-Light Food Chain (e3) is spread over about an hour after sunset, with about 25 minutes of watching. It works best in warm months, and says to look for spiders if no gecko comes. Deer and Tiger Toss (g2) was checked with a computer model of the rules: on one A4 sheet, with deer doubling and tigers needing 2 deer to live and 4 to have a cub, the deer usually rise, then the tigers, then both fall, within 12 rounds. This changed the game from two sheets to one sheet and from 10 to 12 rounds, and added the rule that 2 deer wander in if all are eaten. One Hundred Grains (a2) uses 10 heaps of 10 so a child is not counting 100 grains one by one. Pull One Thread (a4) works with 2 people if toys or chair legs hold the extra cards. Hungry Web (g1) and Journey of a Carbon Atom (a6) can be played alone. Use puffed rice rather than chana, and keep beads away, if a toddler is near. how_we_found_out.story: In the late 1990s, Vibhu Prakash of the Bombay Natural History Society saw that the vultures at Keoladeo, in Bharatpur, were dying. Sick birds sat hunched with drooping heads for weeks, then fell from their perches. Soon vultures were vanishing all over India and Pakistan. Most scientists first thought a new disease was spreading, perhaps a virus, because so many birds died so fast. Others blamed pesticides. A team led by Lindsay Oaks, an American vet working with the Peregrine Fund, examined dead vultures in Pakistan. Most had kidneys that had failed, but the team found no germ that could explain it. So they asked what all the birds had eaten: dead cattle. They tested the birds for medicines given to cattle. They found the painkiller diclofenac in the vultures whose kidneys had failed. Then captive vultures fed meat from a treated animal died in the same way. The answer was published in 2004. The vultures had been poisoned by their food, one step up the food chain.
how_we_found_out.who: Vibhu Prakash of the Bombay Natural History Society, and Lindsay Oaks and his team
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists first thought a new infectious disease, perhaps a virus, was killing the vultures.
